topic: US equity/ETF option assignment, exercise and settlement mechanics for a never-assigned automated system (Alpaca, options level 3, paper, American-style share-settled)

findings.claim: OCC auto-exercises ("exercise by exception") any equity or index option that is ITM by $0.01 or more at expiration, for customer, firm and market-maker accounts alike.
findings.detail: OIC's Options Exercise FAQ states the exercise-by-exception thresholds as $.01 per contract ITM for equity options in customer accounts and $.01 in firm/market-maker accounts, and $.01 for index options across all account types. OIC also stresses that exercise under these procedures is "not, strictly speaking, 'automatic'" — it is a default that clearing members may override with contrary instructions. Alpaca mirrors the $0.01 threshold in its own docs.
findings.why_it_matters: The machine must treat $0.01 ITM as the assignment trigger for any short leg it still holds at expiry — not $0.05, not "a few cents". Any short strike within a cent of the settlement print must be assumed assigned.

findings.claim: Being OTM at the 4:00 pm close does NOT guarantee no assignment. A holder can exercise an OTM option by explicit instruction up to 5:30 pm ET.
findings.detail: FINRA Information Notice 02/03/21: option holders have until "5:30 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) on the day of expiration" to make a final exercise decision; "Members may establish an earlier time to accept exercise instructions ... but may not accept instructions after 5:30 p.m. ET." Exercise-by-exception is only a default; contrary instructions can both suppress an ITM exercise and initiate an OTM one. Alpaca's own support page says of short positions: "If the option expires out-of-the-money then it is likely it will not be exercised. Similarly though, there is a small chance it may be assigned."
findings.why_it_matters: The system must never mark an expiring short leg as "safe, expired worthless" at 16:00 based on the closing price. P&L and risk state for expiring shorts stay PROVISIONAL until the next-session activity feed confirms. No capital may be redeployed against an unconfirmed expiry.

findings.claim: Alpaca states plainly that closing the position before the market close is the ONLY guarantee against assignment.
findings.detail: Verbatim from Alpaca support: "The only way to guarantee that you will not be assigned to the short position is to close out the position prior to the market close." Same page: "You will know before the open the next business day whether you were assigned or not."
findings.why_it_matters: This is the design axiom for a never-assigned system: flatten, do not hedge, do not rely on the long leg, do not rely on OTM-ness. And assignment notification latency is up to overnight, so detection is a next-session reconciliation job, not a real-time guard.

findings.claim: Alpaca's expiration-day cut-offs are early and are documented inconsistently across its own pages. The earliest binding number is 3:15 pm ET.
findings.detail: Alpaca's 0DTE cutoff page: "Orders must be submitted before 3:15 p.m. ET for stocks and options, and before 3:30 p.m. ET for broad-based ETFs like SPY and QQQ." Alpaca docs elsewhere: "Starting at 3:30 pm EST on the date of expiration, Alpaca continuously evaluates any open positions that expire that day and stops accepting new orders to open/extend any positions." The expiration page says "After 4:00:01 PM ET on the expiration date, exercising the option is no longer possible" and that DNE "requests after 4:00 PM ET will be handled on a best-efforts basis, as they must be submitted via email and processed manually" — while another Alpaca page says you have "until 4:30 pm ET" for DNE. Auto-exercise itself "occurs by 6:00 PM ET on expiration day."
findings.why_it_matters: The code must hard-code the most conservative number (3:15 pm ET) as the flatten deadline, not the most generous. The DNE path is manual and email-based, so it is unusable by an automated system and must never appear in a control flow.

findings.claim: Alpaca's documented expiration-day liquidation logic protects the LONG side only. There is no documented Alpaca behaviour that closes a short ITM leg for you.
findings.detail: Alpaca's rules after 3:30 pm ET are described entirely in terms of long positions: if a long call/put is ITM by $0.01+, Alpaca checks buying power (calls) or available shares (puts); if sufficient, it lets auto-exercise happen; if insufficient, "Alpaca will liquidate while it's still ITM" / "sell-out the position within 1 hour before expiry." Searches of the short-position and liquidation pages returned no equivalent protective rule for short legs.
findings.why_it_matters: Absence of evidence here is the finding: do not build any fallback that assumes the broker will rescue a short ITM leg. The bot owns that risk entirely.

findings.claim: The classic spread-breaks scenario: underlying settles BETWEEN the strikes, short leg is ITM and assigned, long leg is OTM and expires worthless, leaving a naked, unhedged share position over the weekend gap.
findings.detail: For a short call spread K_short < K_long, any settlement S with K_short < S < K_long assigns the short call (short 100 shares per contract) while the long call expires worthless. For a short put spread, K_long < S < K_short assigns the short put (long 100 shares per contract, cash owed). The defined-risk graph is only defined risk if both legs resolve together. Alpaca's docs do not describe automatically exercising your long leg to cover an assignment on the short leg.
findings.why_it_matters: Max loss on a vertical is NOT capped when the underlying pins between strikes. The system's risk model must carry a separate, larger "pin loss" number equal to overnight gap risk on strike * 100 * qty of unhedged stock, and the pre-trade sizing check must use that number, not the spread width.

findings.claim: Early assignment on American-style options is economically driven by extrinsic value collapse, and for calls overwhelmingly by dividend capture the day before ex-date.
findings.detail: OIC: "As the ex-date for a dividend approaches, there is increased likelihood that call holders will exercise in-the-money calls" and notes no definitive timing prediction exists. The standard rule of thumb across sources: early exercise becomes rational when the option's remaining extrinsic value is less than the dividend to be captured (calls) or less than the interest earned on the freed strike cash (deep ITM puts). Alpaca: "The holder of the long call options may exercise in order to collect the dividend" and "If the assignment occurs before or on the trading day prior to the underlying security's ex-dividend date, the resulting position may cause you to forfeit the dividend ... or even owe the dividend (if you were assigned on short calls as a part of a spread resulting in a short stock position)."
findings.why_it_matters: Gives a directly computable live signal: extrinsic value per short leg, compared against the next dividend. This is the only forward-looking assignment-risk metric available from market data.

findings.claim: Extrinsic value is computable from Alpaca data WITHOUT greeks, which matters because Alpaca does not return greeks/IV on 0DTE contracts.
findings.detail: extrinsic = option_mid - intrinsic, where intrinsic = max(0, S - K) for a call and max(0, K - S) for a put, S = underlying last/mid. This needs only an option quote and an equity quote, both available on Alpaca at any options level. It does not need IV, delta, or a pricing model. (Consistent with the project's existing note that Alpaca returns no greeks/IV on 0DTE at any tier.)
findings.why_it_matters: The assignment-risk monitor can be built on the quote endpoints alone and will keep working on 0DTE contracts where the greeks feed is empty. Use mid, and reject the reading when the bid/ask spread is wider than the extrinsic value being measured — that measurement is noise.

findings.claim: Alpaca exposes a dividend calendar via the Corporate Actions Announcements API, including ex_date — but with an ingestion lag and known data gaps.
findings.detail: Alpaca's corporate actions API returns announcements with ca_type=Dividend, ca_sub_type=cash, and date fields including declaration date, ex-dividend date, record date and payable date. Alpaca states announcement data is available "typically the following trading day after the declaration date" and that "there may be delays in receiving corporate actions from data providers." Community forum threads report missing dividend announcements.
findings.why_it_matters: The dividend guard can be automated, but it must fail CLOSED: a symbol with no dividend record is not proven to be dividend-free. Treat a lookup miss on a known dividend payer as "ex-date unknown → do not sell calls on it."

findings.claim: Alpaca may itself force-close positions with large dividend risk the day before ex-date, and can impose an "assignment lock" that blocks trading on the underlying.
findings.detail: Alpaca: "Alpaca may take action in your account to close positions that may have large dividend risk exposure on the trading day before the ex-dividend date." Separately, an assignment lock triggers when "you received an assignment on an option position, and your account does not have enough buying power to support the resulting assignment"; the account is then "temporarily restricted from trading option contracts on the same underlying symbol," and the lock is only lifted after the user acts AND contacts support by email or chat.
findings.why_it_matters: Two hard consequences: (1) positions can vanish without the bot ordering it, so the bot must reconcile broker state as truth rather than its own ledger; (2) an assignment lock cannot be cleared programmatically — it requires a human emailing support. The bot must detect order rejections on an underlying, stop retrying, and page a human.

findings.claim: Assignment and exercise events arrive only as non-trade activities over REST — they are NOT pushed over the trade-updates websocket.
findings.detail: Alpaca docs: "options assignments are not delivered through websocket events"; there are NTA entry types OPEXC (exercise), OPASN (assignment) and OPEXP (OTM expiry, where "the Alpaca system will flatten the position"), each accompanied by an OPTRD option-trade activity reflecting the share transaction at the strike.
findings.why_it_matters: The detection path must be a scheduled poll of the account activities endpoint filtered to OPASN/OPEXC/OPEXP/OPTRD. A websocket-only architecture will silently miss every assignment.

findings.claim: On PAPER accounts, option exercise/assignment/expiry activities are synced only at the start of the following day — so a paper environment cannot validate intraday assignment handling.
findings.detail: Alpaca docs: on paper, non-trade activities related to exercise/assignment/expiry are "synced at the start of the following day," though balances and positions update immediately. Whether Alpaca's paper engine simulates EARLY (pre-expiry) assignment at all is not documented anywhere I could find.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the honest limit of paper testing. Passing in paper is not evidence the assignment-handling code works. The reconciliation path must be tested with synthetic injected OPASN records, not by waiting for paper to produce one.

findings.claim: Alpaca's exercise endpoint takes no quantity — it exercises the entire position.
findings.detail: POST /v2/positions/{symbol_or_contract_id}/exercise: Alpaca "will exercise all available held shares" of the contract; requests "submitted between market close and midnight will be rejected." There is no partial-exercise parameter documented.
findings.why_it_matters: A never-assigned system should never call this endpoint. If exercise is ever used defensively (e.g. exercising a long leg to cover an assignment), it is all-or-nothing and cannot be sized to the assigned quantity — which makes it unsuitable as an automated remedy. Remedy the share position with equity orders instead.

findings.claim: Cash-settled European-style index options structurally eliminate early assignment and share delivery — but on Alpaca they are paper-only.
findings.detail: Alpaca supports SPX, SPXW, VIX, VIXW, DJX and XSP: "At expiration, positions settle in cash based on an official reference value. There is no share delivery" and "Exercise happens only at expiration, which removes early assignment during the life of the contract." Availability is "through the Trading API" in "paper trading only" as of that announcement. ETF options (SPY, QQQ, IWM) are American-style and share-settled and carry full assignment risk; XSP is the cash-settled ~1/10-SPX analogue of SPY.
findings.why_it_matters: If the mandate is literally "never be assigned," the structural answer is cash-settled index options, not risk management on share-settled ones. But that path is paper-only today, so a live system still needs the full flatten machinery. Also note AM-settled contracts (standard monthly SPX) settle off the opening prints, so you cannot trade out of the settlement on expiration morning.

findings.claim: Options have expired on the Friday (not Saturday) since February 2015; a lot of older guidance on the web is stale on this.
findings.detail: OCC moved the expiration exercise process to Friday starting June 2013, and after February 1, 2015 virtually all standard expiration contracts expire on Friday itself. The 5:30 pm ET decision window is on expiration Friday, not Saturday. Some currently-published third-party pages still say "options expire Saturday at 11:59 am ET" — that is wrong.
findings.why_it_matters: Calendar logic must use the Friday expiration date, and the exercise-uncertainty window is 16:00–17:30 ET Friday, not a weekend-long window. Do not implement against blog-sourced Saturday semantics.

findings.claim: Half days and modified closes shift every deadline, and the exercise-decision window shifts with them.
findings.detail: FINRA/OCC amendments extend the deadline for a final exercise decision on an expiring standardized option to one hour and thirty minutes following a modified closing time. US half days close at 1:00 pm ET.
findings.why_it_matters: Deadlines must be computed from the exchange calendar's actual close for that date, never hard-coded to 16:00/17:30. A 1:00 pm close means the flatten deadline moves to roughly 12:15 pm ET and the exercise window runs to 2:30 pm ET.

findings.claim: The probability that a specific short leg gets assigned early cannot be computed from available data. Any number the system produces is a heuristic, not a probability.
findings.detail: OIC explicitly declines to predict early-exercise timing, noting holders weigh intrinsic value against forfeited time value. There is no public per-contract, per-account feed of exercise notices, no visibility into who holds the long side, and OCC allocation to clearing members is random with firms then allocating to customers by their own (random or FIFO) method. Assignment can also be partial — e.g. 1 of 10 contracts.
findings.why_it_matters: Do not build a probability-threshold gate ("close if P(assign) > 15%"), because the input does not exist. Build deterministic trigger gates on observable quantities instead: extrinsic value, dividend calendar, moneyness, clock. And handle PARTIAL assignment — the code must not assume a position goes from full size to zero.

findings.claim: Deep-ITM short puts are the weakest-evidence early-assignment channel and the guidance is rate-dependent.
findings.detail: The theory is that a put holder exercises early when remaining extrinsic value falls below the interest earnable on the strike proceeds — so deep ITM, low extrinsic, high short rates and longer remaining time all increase it. Unlike the dividend/call case, I found no broker or OCC document giving a concrete numeric trigger, and the effect scales with the prevailing risk-free rate, which the system does not receive from Alpaca.
findings.why_it_matters: State this honestly rather than encoding a fake rule: the put-side trigger should be a pure extrinsic-value floor (close when extrinsic is at or near zero), not a rate model the system cannot parameterise.

rules_for_the_machine: FLATTEN DEADLINE (hard): no short leg on any American-style, share-settled option may be open after 15:00:00 ET on its expiration date. At 14:45 ET submit the closing order; at 14:55 ET if unfilled, reprice to marketable; at 15:05 ET if still unfilled, send a market order; at 15:12 ET if still open, raise a critical page. Rationale: Alpaca rejects 0DTE orders after 15:15 ET for single-name options and 15:30 ET for broad-based ETFs, and stops accepting opening/extending orders at 15:30 ET.

ALL DEADLINES FROM THE EXCHANGE CALENDAR: compute every expiration-day deadline as (session_close - 60 min), never as a hard-coded wall-clock time. On a 13:00 ET half-day close the flatten deadline is 12:00 ET. Reject the trading day entirely if the calendar lookup fails.

NEVER CALL THE EXERCISE ENDPOINT. POST /v2/positions/{id}/exercise has no quantity parameter and exercises the whole position. Remediate any assigned share position with ordinary equity orders instead. Assert this at the HTTP-client layer: block the URL pattern.
NEVER DEPEND ON DO-NOT-EXERCISE. Alpaca DNE is submitted by email and processed manually, best-efforts after 16:00 ET. No code path may branch on 'submit DNE'. It is a human escape hatch only.

CLOSE SPREADS ATOMICALLY: exit a multi-leg position with a single mleg order. If the broker rejects the mleg close and leg-by-leg is required, close the SHORT leg first and only then the long leg. Never allow a state where the long leg is closed and the short leg is open — assert this invariant after every fill and halt the strategy if it is violated.

NO 0DTE SHORT LEGS unless explicitly enabled per-underlying. If enabled, no new short leg may be opened on an expiring contract after 11:00 ET, and the 15:00 ET flatten rule still applies with no exception for profitability.

PIN-RISK BAND: at 14:30 ET on expiration day, for every short strike K with underlying price S, if |S - K| <= max(0.005 * S, $0.50), flatten the entire spread immediately at market regardless of P&L. Re-evaluate every 60 seconds until 15:00 ET; the band widens rather than narrows as the clock runs.
ASSIGNMENT-IS-$0.01: everywhere the code asks 'is this leg at risk', the ITM test is (S - K) >= 0.01 for calls and (K - S) >= 0.01 for puts. Do not use a wider tolerance to mean 'safe'.

OTM IS NOT SAFE: never mark an expiring short leg as settled/worthless based on the 16:00 ET price. Hold expiring short positions in state PENDING_EXPIRY_CONFIRMATION until the next-session activity poll confirms. No capital freed by a pending expiry may be reused for new positions.

EXTRINSIC MONITOR (every cycle, all short legs): extrinsic = option_mid - max(0, S-K) for calls, option_mid - max(0, K-S) for puts. If extrinsic <= $0.05, mark EARLY_ASSIGNMENT_RISK=HIGH and close the spread the same cycle. If the option bid/ask spread exceeds the computed extrinsic, treat the reading as unreliable, mark it STALE, and close on the conservative assumption rather than trusting the number.

DIVIDEND GUARD (short calls): run a pre-open job that queries the Alpaca corporate actions announcements API for ca_type=Dividend on every underlying with an open or candidate short call. If ex_date is within the next 2 trading sessions AND the short call is ITM, flatten by 15:00 ET on the session BEFORE ex_date. Additionally flatten if extrinsic < dividend_per_share regardless of moneyness.

DIVIDEND GUARD FAILS CLOSED: if the corporate-actions lookup errors, returns empty for a symbol not on a verified no-dividend whitelist, or returns data older than 2 days, treat the symbol as having an unknown ex-date and block any new short call on it. Alpaca's announcement feed has documented ingestion lag and gaps.

NO SHORT CALLS INTO EX-DATE: hard block on opening any short call leg on a dividend-paying underlying within 5 sessions of a known ex_date unless extrinsic value at entry exceeds 3x the expected dividend per share.

DEEP-ITM PUT FLOOR: close any short put whose extrinsic <= $0.05, at any DTE. Do not attempt to model the interest-rate-driven early-exercise boundary — the system has no risk-free-rate input and the evidence for a numeric trigger is weak.

SIZE FOR ASSIGNMENT, NOT FOR SPREAD WIDTH: before opening any spread, verify the account can absorb full assignment of the short leg as a stock position — strike * 100 * qty of buying-power impact for short puts, and the equivalent short-stock requirement for short calls — without triggering a margin call. If not, reduce quantity. Never size a position on the assumption that max loss equals spread width.

ASSIGNMENT RECONCILIATION JOB: poll GET /v2/account/activities for activity types OPASN, OPEXC, OPEXP and OPTRD at 08:00 ET, 09:00 ET, and every 15 minutes during the session. Do not rely on the trade-updates websocket — Alpaca does not push assignments over it.

ON OPASN DETECTED: immediately (a) halt new order generation for that underlying, (b) flatten the resulting share position at the next available liquid moment, (c) reconcile the ledger against GET /v2/positions as the source of truth rather than internal state, (d) page a human. Handle PARTIAL assignment: the assigned quantity may be less than the position size.

BROKER STATE IS TRUTH: before every order-generation cycle, diff internal position state against GET /v2/positions. Alpaca can unilaterally liquidate ITM longs near expiry and can close positions with large dividend-risk exposure the day before ex-date. Any unexplained diff halts trading and pages.

ASSIGNMENT LOCK IS NOT RECOVERABLE IN CODE: if orders on an underlying start rejecting after an assignment event, stop retrying after 2 attempts, mark the underlying DISABLED, and page — the lock is only lifted after a human contacts Alpaca support.

PAPER DOES NOT VALIDATE THIS: on paper accounts Alpaca syncs option exercise/assignment/expiry activities only at the start of the following day, and early-assignment simulation is undocumented. Test the OPASN handling path with injected synthetic activity records in an integration test; never treat a clean paper run as evidence the assignment path works.

IF 'NEVER ASSIGNED' IS ABSOLUTE, PREFER CASH-SETTLED EUROPEAN INDEX OPTIONS (SPX/SPXW/XSP/VIX on Alpaca): no early exercise, no share delivery. Note these are paper-only on Alpaca today, and that AM-settled monthlies settle off opening prints, so an expiration-morning exit is not possible for them — flatten the session before.

DAILY INVARIANT ASSERTION at 15:20 ET: count of open short legs on share-settled options expiring today must equal zero. If not zero, the system is in a failed state: page immediately and do not start the next session's strategy logic until a human clears it.

topic: Risk management and position sizing for a fully automated multi-strategy options book (Alpaca, options level 3, ~$50k paper account, US equities/ETFs, American-style share-settled)

findings.claim: Alpaca's margin for a multi-leg order is computed from the worst-case intrinsic payoff, ignoring premium — so defined max loss and broker buying-power reduction are the same number, and sizing by 'max loss' and sizing by 'buying power' collapse into one calculation.
findings.detail: Alpaca documents a 'universal spread rule': premiums are ignored, each leg is modeled as a piecewise-linear exercise payoff, the payoffs are summed, and maintenance margin = |worst-case net payoff|. For multiple expirations it is computed per expiration and the largest is used. Cost basis of an MLeg order = maintenance margin + (net premium x 100). Offsetting spreads can net to $0 margin. Alpaca also accepts an MLeg order ONLY if every leg is covered within that same order — no uncovered short legs, no rolling of naked shorts, no calendar spreads inside one MLeg order, and no equity leg mixed in.
findings.why_it_matters: The sizing engine needs exactly one risk number per position: width_points x 100 x contracts - credit_received (for a vertical). It must compute this locally and pre-check it against remaining risk budget BEFORE submitting, because Alpaca will reject or silently reserve differently than a naive 'premium x contracts' estimate. It must also never attempt to construct a position as legs-in-sequence (which would momentarily be naked and get rejected or, worse, partially fill).

findings.claim: A 'defined-risk' spread is only defined-risk while both legs are alive. Early assignment on the short leg converts the position into a stock position plus a long option, and the realized loss can exceed the stated max loss.
findings.detail: American-style equity/ETF options can be assigned at any time, at any ITM amount. Assignment on a short call leaves the account short 100 shares per contract; if the assignment happens on or before the ex-dividend date the account owes the dividend (100 x dividend per contract), which is an out-of-pocket cost on top of the spread's max loss. Alpaca states assignment 'occurs randomly overnight when short positions are in-the-money' and generates OPASN + OPTRD activities. The long leg still caps directional risk only if it is exercised or the stock is covered promptly — overnight the account carries unhedged share risk.
findings.why_it_matters: The machine cannot treat max-loss as a hard ceiling. It needs an assignment detector that runs on every activity poll, a same-session flatten routine for delivered shares, an ex-dividend blackout on short ITM calls, and a risk budget that assumes max_loss can be exceeded by roughly (dividend + one overnight gap on the delivered shares).

findings.claim: Alpaca stops accepting opening orders on expiration day at 3:30 pm ET and will itself liquidate or auto-exercise your expiring positions — the broker takes control of the position before the machine's own end-of-day logic would.
findings.detail: Alpaca support states order cutoffs on expiration day of 3:15 pm ET for stocks/single equities and 3:30 pm ET for broad-based ETFs (SPY, QQQ); orders after those times are rejected. From 3:30 pm ET Alpaca continuously evaluates open positions expiring that day and stops accepting orders that open or extend positions. If a long position is ITM by $0.01+ Alpaca checks for buying power (calls) or shares (puts); if sufficient it lets it auto-exercise, if not it liquidates the option while still ITM. OTM positions are flattened. ITM covered calls and cash-secured puts auto-assign after the close.
findings.why_it_matters: Every close-out deadline in the code must be strictly earlier than the broker's cutoff, with margin for retries and partial fills. A 'close at 3:45' rule is unimplementable. This also means the machine must never rely on being able to defend a position in the last 30 minutes of expiration day.

findings.claim: OCC exercise-by-exception is $0.01 ITM for equity and index options, and the broker may use a different threshold — so 'it expired worthless' is never a safe assumption for a short leg that closed near the strike.
findings.detail: OCC thresholds: $0.01 per contract ITM in customer accounts for equity options; $0.01 in all account types for index options. OCC explicitly notes a firm may have a different threshold, that exercise-by-exception is an administrative convenience rather than truly automatic, and that clearing members can choose not to exercise or to exercise below threshold. The exchange deadline for exercise notices is 4:30 pm CT, after the underlying has stopped trading — the holder of the long option gets to decide after seeing post-close moves.
findings.why_it_matters: Pin risk is a real, asymmetric cost: a short leg within a few cents of the money at the close can be assigned or not, and the machine will not know until the next morning. The code needs a hard rule to close (not hold) any short leg whose strike is within a defined distance of spot before the cutoff, rather than modeling the probability of assignment.

findings.claim: Systematically selling index premium has produced roughly a one-third drawdown in a real, published, rules-based benchmark — so 'defined risk per trade' does not bound portfolio drawdown.
findings.detail: Cboe research (Bondarenko, 2019) on the Cboe S&P 500 PutWrite Index (PUT) reports maximum drawdown of -32.7% for PUT vs -50.9% for the S&P 500 over the studied window. PUT is fully collateralized, monthly, at-the-money, and mechanically executed — i.e. about as risk-controlled as a short-premium program gets, and it still lost roughly a third.
findings.why_it_matters: Capital-at-risk limits must be set from an assumed portfolio drawdown of at least 30%, not from per-trade max loss. A book whose per-trade losses are 'only 2%' can still stack correlated losses into a 30% hole. This is the empirical anchor for the total-risk-deployed cap.

findings.claim: Kelly sizing is actively dangerous for a short-premium book: the standard Kelly formula assumes a distribution that short options do not have, and it systematically oversizes negatively-skewed bets.
findings.detail: Kelly derived under normal/variance assumptions overestimates the optimal position for negatively skewed payoffs; this is cited as a structural reason short-vol vehicles failed in February 2018. Practitioner and academic consensus is to treat full Kelly as a theoretical ceiling and use 1/4 to 1/2 Kelly. An arXiv study applying Kelly to S&P 500 put-writing (2508.16598) reports drawdowns exceeding 60-80% for at-the-money Kelly-sized positions, versus roughly 9-11% out-of-sample drawdown for a hybrid Kelly/VIX-scaled configuration on far-OTM short-dated options — and it applies full Kelly throughout without a clean fractional-Kelly comparison, so it does not establish an optimal fraction.
findings.why_it_matters: The machine should not implement Kelly as its sizing rule. If Kelly is computed at all it should be a monitor that can only reduce size, capped at 1/4 Kelly, and only after enough live trades exist to estimate edge — which for a strategy with a ~75% win rate needs hundreds of trades, not dozens.

findings.claim: The 50%-of-credit profit target and 21-DTE management rule are trading-house conventions from a single vendor's proprietary, non-replicable research — the mechanism is plausible, the published evidence is weak.
findings.detail: The 50% and 21-DTE conventions originate in tastytrade's own backtests. The specific figures circulating ('200,000 credit spread trades', '45 DTE entries managed at 21 DTE produced the highest risk-adjusted returns') come from third-party blogs (daystoexpiry.com, optionalpha.com) citing tastytrade, not from a published paper with data, methodology, or out-of-sample testing. No peer-reviewed independent replication was found. The mechanism — gamma rises and theta's compensation falls as expiry approaches, so late-life risk/reward deteriorates — is sound and is standard options math. But the specific numbers 50% and 21 are not derived from theory and are plausibly the product of selection over many tested thresholds. Backtest critiques note these studies typically assume mid-price fills and ignore slippage and fees, which disproportionately flatters frequent-close rules.
findings.why_it_matters: Implement 50%/21-DTE as configurable parameters with defaults, not as truths. The machine must log its own realized fills against the assumption so the convention can be falsified on this account's own data; and the profit target must be expressed net of the actual cost to close (bid/ask), not on mid.

findings.claim: Stop-losses on credit spreads expressed as a multiple of credit (commonly 2x) are a convention with no strong published evidence, and on a defined-risk spread they are partly redundant and partly harmful.
findings.detail: The widely quoted rule is 'close winners at 50% of credit, stop out if the credit doubles' (i.e. loss = 1x credit, exit price = 2x credit). No primary study with data supporting 2x over 1.5x or 3x was located. Two structural problems: (a) on a defined-risk vertical, max loss is already bounded, so a stop converts a bounded loss into a realized loss more often — it raises the loss frequency to lower loss severity, which is a variance choice, not an edge; (b) a stop keyed to option price is a market order into a widening spread precisely when the market is stressed, and short-option quotes gap. For a 1-wide spread sold at $0.33, a 2x stop triggers at $0.66 for a $33 loss vs a $67 max loss — it saves only half the remaining risk while paying the spread.
findings.why_it_matters: If a stop is used, it must be a limit-based, marketable-with-cap exit, must be skipped when the quoted spread exceeds a threshold, and must be evaluated on the spread's mark rather than on a single leg. The honest default is: rely on the defined max loss and on position count limits, and use the 2x rule only as a de-risking preference, not as a safety mechanism.

findings.claim: Portfolio greek caps for a ~$50k account have no authoritative published source. Any specific number is a judgement call and must be presented as such.
findings.detail: No regulator, exchange, or peer-reviewed source prescribes net delta / vega / gamma limits for a retail account. What IS checkable: Alpaca returns no greeks or IV for 0DTE contracts at any tier (already recorded in this project's own reference notes), so the machine must compute greeks locally from a pricing model with intraday time-to-expiry. That means the greek limits are enforced against the machine's OWN estimates, whose error grows exactly when it matters (high vol, near expiry, wide quotes).
findings.why_it_matters: Greek limits are still worth enforcing — they are the only thing that catches an accidentally one-sided book — but they must be treated as soft guardrails with conservative caps, and the machine must degrade safely (refuse to open) when a greek cannot be computed, rather than assuming zero.
findings.source: reasoning; Alpaca greeks gap recorded in C:\Users\Cole\.claude\projects\C--Users-Cole\memory\reference_alpaca_0dte_greeks_gap.md

findings.claim: Concurrent positions on the same underlying are not diversification, and positions on different underlyings are far more correlated than their symbols suggest.
findings.detail: Two credit spreads on SPY at different strikes/expiries are one bet on SPY with a non-linear payoff; in a gap they lose together. Across underlyings, equity correlations converge toward 1 in stress: on 5 Feb 2018 the S&P 500 fell 4.1% and VIX rose ~116% in one day (largest percentage move since 1993 at the time); on 5 Aug 2024 VIX spiked ~180% intraday to ~65, the largest one-day VIX spike on record, with the S&P down ~3-4% and small caps -5.5% at the open. A book of 'diversified' short-premium positions on SPY, QQQ, IWM and large-cap single names is one short-vol position.
findings.why_it_matters: Risk must be aggregated by underlying AND by beta-weighted exposure to a market proxy, not counted as N independent positions. The limit that binds should be total risk deployed and beta-weighted delta, with per-underlying concentration as a sub-limit.

findings.claim: The $25,000 pattern-day-trader minimum was eliminated effective 4 June 2026 and replaced by intraday margin monitoring under amended FINRA Rule 4210 — but brokers have until 20 October 2027 to comply, so Alpaca's actual behaviour must be verified, not assumed.
findings.detail: FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10: SEC approved the amendments 20 April 2026, effective 4 June 2026, with an extended compliance date of 20 October 2027. PDT designation and the $25,000 minimum are gone; margin accounts revert to the $2,000 minimum equity requirement. Firms must determine an 'intraday margin deficit' for each margin account when intraday-margin-level-reducing transactions occur, using either real-time monitoring or a single end-of-day calculation.
findings.why_it_matters: The machine should not hard-code PDT day-trade counting as a constraint, but it also must not assume unlimited intraday round trips are free — intraday margin monitoring can produce a deficit call mid-day. The code should read Alpaca's account fields (daytrade_count, daytrading_buying_power, and any new intraday fields) each cycle and halt on any restriction flag rather than modeling the rule.

findings.claim: Paper trading will systematically understate this book's risk, because the failure modes that hurt most — early assignment, fill quality on wide spreads, and liquidation during stress — are the ones a paper engine simulates least faithfully.
findings.detail: Alpaca enables options in paper by default and supports level 3 there. Alpaca's documentation describes automatic exercise, expiry and assignment activities but does not document how (or whether) early assignment is simulated in paper; community questions on exactly this point are unanswered in the docs. European-style index options cannot be early-assigned at all, so index paper results say nothing about American-style equity/ETF assignment risk. Paper fills also do not experience queue position or liquidity withdrawal.
findings.why_it_matters: Any statistic the machine derives from paper performance — win rate, average loss, realized slippage, Kelly inputs — is biased optimistic. The system must carry an explicit slippage and assignment penalty in its own accounting, and must never promote a parameter to live on paper results alone.

findings.claim: A gap against a defined-risk position is a state where the correct automated action is usually to do nothing mechanical and to stop opening — not to exit at market.
findings.detail: When the underlying gaps through a short strike, three things are simultaneously true: the spread is already near max loss (so the remaining risk being 'saved' by exiting is small), option quotes are at their widest (so the exit cost is at its highest), and the position's remaining value is mostly intrinsic (so time-based recovery is limited but not zero). Exiting at market in that state realizes the widest spread of the day. This cannot be resolved with certainty from available data — whether holding to expiry beats exiting at the gap depends on the underlying's post-gap drift, which is not reliably predictable.
findings.why_it_matters: The gap handler must be a separate code path from the normal stop, must use limit orders with a defined max giveup relative to the theoretical value, must have an attempt budget, and must escalate to a human alert rather than looping. It must also immediately trip the open-new-positions block for the rest of the session.

findings.claim: Alpaca's own documented order surface constrains what risk controls are even expressible: options are day-only, market and limit only, no extended hours, no bracket/OTO orders, and multi-leg exits must themselves be valid covered MLeg orders.
findings.detail: Alpaca docs: options support market and limit orders only, time-in-force 'day' only, no extended hours, no fractional/notional. Bracket and OTO order classes are not supported for options. Multi-leg orders require order_class 'mleg', leg ratios in simplest form (GCD 1), all legs on the same underlying, and all legs covered within the order.
findings.why_it_matters: There is no broker-side stop or bracket to fall back on. Every exit — profit target, stop, time stop, kill switch — must be actively managed by the machine's own polling loop. That makes process liveness itself a risk control: if the process dies, nothing protects the book. A watchdog and a documented manual-flatten procedure are part of the risk system, not optional extras.

findings.claim: Daily loss limits and kill switches only work if they are keyed to an account-level number the broker reports, latched persistently, and require a human to clear.
findings.detail: Self-computed P&L drifts from broker-reported equity through unrecorded assignments, fees, corporate actions and partial fills. Alpaca exposes account equity and last_equity on the trading account endpoint; option events appear as non-trade activities (OPEXC, OPASN, OPEXP) that a naive position-based P&L will miss entirely. A kill switch that is recomputed from strategy state on restart is not a kill switch — a crash-and-restart clears it.
findings.why_it_matters: The daily-loss check must compare broker equity to a start-of-day snapshot stored on disk, the tripped state must be written to durable storage with a timestamp and reason, and startup must read that state before doing anything else. Auto-reset at midnight is acceptable only for a soft limit; the hard limit must require explicit human clearance.

findings.claim: What an automated system must refuse to do is a shorter and more important list than what it may do, and several items on it are structural rather than discretionary.
findings.detail: Refusals divide into: (1) things the broker will reject anyway (uncovered legs in an MLeg order, orders after the expiry-day cutoff, equity legs in an MLeg order); (2) things that are legal but convert defined risk into undefined risk (holding delivered shares overnight, letting an ITM short leg go to expiry, exercising a long leg to 'save' a spread without flattening the resulting shares); (3) things that are legal and bounded but destroy the system's ability to be reasoned about (sizing up after losses, overriding its own kill switch, opening a position it has no tested exit path for, trading a contract whose quote it cannot value); and (4) things no automated system should ever do without a human: change its own risk limits, move money, or trade a symbol not on an explicit allowlist.
findings.why_it_matters: Each refusal is a guard clause that runs before order submission. They should be implemented as a single pre-trade gate function that every strategy must pass through, returning a reason string, with every rejection logged — so a strategy cannot bypass risk by constructing orders itself.

rules_for_the_machine: SIZING — single risk number: For every candidate position compute defined_max_loss locally before submission. For a vertical: (width_in_points * 100 * contracts) - (net_credit * 100 * contracts). For any multi-leg, evaluate the piecewise payoff at every strike and at 0 and 2x spot, and take |worst net payoff|. Reject any position for which this number cannot be computed in closed form. Never size from premium collected.

SIZING — per-position cap: defined_max_loss <= 1.0% of start-of-day account equity. At $50k that is $500 per position. Hard reject above; no override flag in code. Rationale: this is a judgement call, not a derived optimum — it is chosen so that ~30 consecutive maximum losses (the empirical PUT-index drawdown scale) does not end the account.
SIZING — per-underlying cap: sum of defined_max_loss across all open positions on one underlying <= 2.0% of equity ($1,000 at $50k). Aggregate by underlying symbol, not by contract.

SIZING — total deployed cap: sum of defined_max_loss across the entire book <= 10% of equity ($5,000 at $50k). Reject any new order that would breach it. This is the binding constraint most of the time and should be the first check.

SIZING — never Kelly as the sizer: Do not compute position size from the Kelly criterion. If a Kelly estimate is computed at all, it may only be used as a multiplier in [0, 0.25] applied to the cap above, may never increase size above the cap, and must be disabled until at least 300 closed trades exist on the same strategy and underlying. Kelly under normal assumptions oversizes negatively-skewed payoffs.

SIZING — no martingale: Position size must be a pure function of current equity and the caps above. It must never reference recent P&L, loss streaks, or 'recovery' targets. Assert in code that the sizing function does not read the trade history.
SIZING — minimum viable size: If the computed contract count rounds to 0, do not open the position. Never round up to 1.

GREEKS — compute locally: Alpaca returns no greeks or IV on 0DTE at any tier. Compute all greeks locally using intraday time-to-expiry in years (not whole days). If a greek cannot be computed for any open or candidate leg, treat the portfolio greek check as FAILED, not as zero.

GREEKS — beta-weighted net delta: Beta-weight every position's delta to SPY and cap |net portfolio beta-weighted delta| at 0.30 * (equity / SPY_price) shares-equivalent — at $50k with SPY near $600 that is about +/-25 SPY-equivalent deltas, i.e. a 1% SPY move moves the book about $150. Reject any order that would breach it. This cap is a convention with no authoritative source; log it as a tunable.

GREEKS — net vega: Cap net portfolio vega at -0.10% of equity per vol point (about -$50 per 1 vol point at $50k) and at +0.05% on the long side. A short-premium book will run short vega; the cap exists so a VIX move of 20 points (observed twice in the last decade: +20 pts on 2018-02-05, +40 pts on 2024-08-05) costs at most ~$1,000 in vega terms.

GREEKS — gamma: Cap |net portfolio gamma| such that the change in net beta-weighted delta from a 2% adverse SPY move stays inside the delta cap above. Implement as: simulate spot -2% and +2%, recompute net delta, reject the order if either simulated net delta breaches the delta cap.
GREEKS — theta is not a limit: Do not set a minimum theta target. A theta floor is an incentive to sell more premium and inverts the purpose of the risk system. Report theta; never gate on it.

CONCURRENCY — max concurrent positions: <= 8 open multi-leg positions total, and <= 3 on any single underlying. Count a multi-leg position as one position. These are operational limits (what the machine can monitor and exit within one polling cycle), not statistical ones.

CONCURRENCY — correlation is not diversification: Positions on different underlyings do not relax the total-deployed cap. Do not implement any rule that increases allowed size because positions are on different symbols.

CONCURRENCY — allowlist only: Trade only symbols on an explicit, human-maintained allowlist stored in config. Reject every symbol not on it, including symbols returned by a scanner. No dynamic universe expansion at runtime.

DAILY LOSS — key to broker equity: At the first successful poll of each session, snapshot account equity from Alpaca's trading account endpoint to durable storage with the date. All intraday loss checks compare current broker-reported equity to that snapshot, never to internally computed P&L.
DAILY LOSS — soft limit: If (snapshot_equity - current_equity) >= 2% of snapshot_equity, stop opening new positions for the rest of the session. Managing and closing existing positions continues.

DAILY LOSS — hard kill switch: If (snapshot_equity - current_equity) >= 4% of snapshot_equity, cancel all working orders, stop opening anything, write a latched HALTED state to disk with timestamp and reason, and alert a human. Do not auto-liquidate — liquidating into a stressed tape is itself a loss event.

KILL SWITCH — durability: The halted state must be written to a file or database, not held in memory. On every startup, read it BEFORE connecting to the broker or evaluating any strategy. A halt cleared by a restart is not a halt.

KILL SWITCH — human clearance: The hard halt may only be cleared by a human action (a file edit, a CLI command with an explicit confirmation, or a dashboard button). No time-based auto-reset, no auto-clear at midnight.

KILL SWITCH — additional trip conditions, each latching the halt: (a) more than 3 order rejections from Alpaca in 60 seconds; (b) any unexpected share position appearing in the account (assignment); (c) market data staleness > 60 seconds during RTH; (d) any account restriction flag from Alpaca (account_blocked, trading_blocked, transfers_blocked, or a liquidation-only restriction); (e) an unhandled exception in the main loop.

WATCHDOG — process liveness is a risk control: Alpaca supports no bracket or OTO orders for options and no GTC — every exit is managed by this process. Run a watchdog that alerts a human if the main loop has not completed a cycle in 120 seconds during RTH. Document a manual flatten procedure that a human can run without the bot.

PROFIT TAKING — 50% target, net of the real exit cost: Close a credit spread when it can be closed at or below 50% of the credit received, evaluated against the NATURAL price (what it would actually cost to close), not the mid. Implement as a limit order at 50% of credit, repriced toward the natural on a schedule, with a maximum giveup. Treat 50% as a config parameter with a logged default, not a constant.

PROFIT TAKING — evidence caveat in code: Annotate the 50% and 21-DTE parameters in config with a comment stating that their published support is a single vendor's proprietary backtests without independent replication, and that the machine logs its own realized outcomes so the parameters can be re-fit on this account's data.

TIME STOP — 21 DTE: Close any short-premium position at 21 calendar days to expiration regardless of P&L, using a limit order with a defined giveup. The mechanism (gamma rises, theta compensation falls in the final weeks) is sound options math; the specific number 21 is a convention. If a 21-DTE close cannot be filled inside the giveup, escalate to alert rather than crossing the spread.

STOP LOSS — express as credit multiple, but as a limit and with a liquidity guard: If a stop is enabled, trigger when the spread's mark reaches 2.0x the credit received (i.e. an unrealized loss of 1.0x credit). Submit a limit order, never a market order. SKIP the stop entirely and hold to the defined max loss if the spread's quoted bid/ask is wider than 20% of the spread's mark, or if either leg has no bid. A stop that pays an unbounded spread is worse than the bounded loss it was meant to avoid.
STOP LOSS — never on a single leg: Evaluate and exit the position as a whole via an MLeg order. Never close one leg of a vertical, which converts a defined-risk position into an undefined-risk one.

GAP HANDLING — separate code path: When the underlying has gapped through a short strike (spread mark >= 80% of max loss at the first poll of the session), do NOT run the normal stop. Instead: (1) immediately set the no-new-positions flag for the session; (2) compute the position's theoretical value from local greeks; (3) attempt a limit close with a maximum giveup of 5% of the spread width, repricing at most 3 times over 10 minutes; (4) if unfilled, hold, alert a human, and re-evaluate next cycle. Log every attempt. It cannot be determined from available data whether holding or exiting is better after a gap; the rule optimizes for not paying the widest spread of the day and for putting a human in the loop.

EXPIRY — close before the broker's cutoff, with margin: Close or roll every expiring position no later than 3:00 pm ET on expiration day for single equities and 3:15 pm ET for SPY/QQQ. Alpaca rejects orders after 3:15 pm ET (equities) and 3:30 pm ET (broad-based ETFs) and takes control of expiring positions from 3:30 pm ET. Never schedule an action inside the broker's window.

EXPIRY — pin-risk rule: Never carry a short leg into expiration when |spot - short_strike| < 1.0% of spot. OCC exercise-by-exception is $0.01 ITM, the exercise-notice deadline is 4:30 pm CT (after the underlying stops trading), brokers may use different thresholds, and holders may choose either way. Close the position instead of predicting assignment.

ASSIGNMENT — detect every cycle: Poll the account activities endpoint for OPASN, OPEXC and OPEXP events every cycle and reconcile positions against the broker's reported positions, not against internal state. Any share position the machine did not intend is an assignment.

ASSIGNMENT — flatten delivered shares same session: On detecting assignment, immediately flatten the resulting share position during regular hours (there are no extended hours for options at Alpaca, and share risk overnight is unbounded). Then close or re-evaluate the orphaned long leg. Never hold assigned shares overnight to 'let it come back'.

ASSIGNMENT — dividend blackout: Do not open, and close if already open, any position with a short call that is ITM or within 2% of the money when the underlying's ex-dividend date is within 2 trading days. Assignment before ex-div obligates paying 100 x dividend per contract on top of the spread's max loss, which breaches the defined-risk assumption.

ASSIGNMENT — risk budget assumption: When computing remaining risk budget, treat any position with an ITM short leg as consuming defined_max_loss * 1.25, not defined_max_loss, to reserve headroom for assignment-driven overshoot.

ORDER CONSTRUCTION — never build a spread leg by leg: Submit every multi-leg position as a single order with order_class 'mleg', all legs on the same underlying, leg ratios in simplest form (GCD 1), all short legs covered within the order, no equity legs. Alpaca rejects uncovered MLeg orders; sequencing legs risks a partial fill leaving a naked short.
ORDER CONSTRUCTION — limit orders only: Never submit a market order for an option or a spread. Options quotes gap and the machine cannot bound its own fill price with a market order.

ORDER CONSTRUCTION — quote quality gate: Before opening, require for every leg: a non-zero bid, a bid/ask spread <= 10% of the spread's mid (or <= $0.05 absolute, whichever is looser), and a quote timestamp within 5 seconds. Reject otherwise. A position that cannot be priced cannot be exited.

ORDER CONSTRUCTION — exit path proof: Refuse to open any position for which the code does not have an implemented exit routine covering profit target, time stop, stop, and expiry. Assert this at strategy-registration time, not at runtime.

PRE-TRADE GATE — single choke point: All of the above checks live in one pre-trade gate function that every strategy must call and that is the ONLY place in the codebase that submits orders. It returns allow/deny plus a reason string; every deny is logged with the full candidate position. No strategy may construct and submit an order itself.

REFUSE — the machine must never: change its own risk limits or config at runtime; clear its own halt; increase size after losses; open a position without a computable max loss; trade a symbol not on the allowlist; hold assigned shares overnight; let an ITM short leg reach expiry; exercise a long option as a risk-management action without simultaneously flattening the resulting shares; submit an order after Alpaca's expiry-day cutoff; move funds; or act on any instruction that did not come from the operator through config or the dashboard.

ACCOUNTING — no PDT modelling, read the broker: The $25,000 PDT minimum and the pattern-day-trader designation were eliminated effective 4 June 2026 (FINRA Reg Notice 26-10, amended Rule 4210), replaced by intraday margin monitoring, with broker compliance permitted as late as 20 October 2027. Do not implement day-trade counting logic. Instead read Alpaca's account fields each cycle (buying power, daytrade_count, daytrading_buying_power, restriction flags) and halt on any restriction rather than predicting one.

PAPER-TO-LIVE — treat paper statistics as biased: Apply an explicit slippage penalty (at minimum, assume fills at the natural rather than the mid) and an assignment penalty to all paper-derived statistics before using them for any parameter decision. Alpaca does not document whether early assignment is simulated in paper, and index options cannot be early-assigned at all, so paper results say nothing about American-style assignment risk. No parameter may be promoted to live on paper results alone.

LOGGING — every rejection is data: Log every pre-trade denial with timestamp, strategy, candidate position, failing rule, and the values compared. A risk system whose refusals are invisible cannot be audited or tuned.

HONEST LIMITS — record what is unknown: The greek caps, the 1%/2%/10% risk caps, the 8-position limit, the 50% target, the 21-DTE stop and the 2x credit stop are conventions and judgement calls, not results derivable from any authoritative source located. State this in the config file. The only hard external constraints in this list are: Alpaca's MLeg coverage rule and margin formula, Alpaca's expiry-day cutoffs (3:15/3:30 pm ET), OCC's $0.01 exercise-by-exception threshold and 4:30 pm CT notice deadline, American-style early assignment, and the elimination of the PDT rule on 4 June 2026.

topic: Options market microstructure and execution quality for an automated retail system (Alpaca, options L3, SPY/QQQ, American/share-settled)

findings.claim: SPY and QQQ options quote in $0.01 increments at every price — the $0.05-above-$3.00 penny-program rule does not apply to them.
findings.detail: Cboe Rule 5.4 (Penny Interval Program) sets $0.01 below $3.00 and $0.05 at/above $3.00 for penny classes, and $0.05/$0.10 for non-penny classes. SPY, QQQ and IWM are carved out at $0.01 for all series regardless of price. I confirmed this live rather than from memory: the broker chain metadata for both SPY and QQQ returns min_ticks = {above_tick: 0.01, below_tick: 0.01, cutoff_price: 0.00} on every contract I pulled (0DTE, 3DTE and 28DTE). Consequence: the NBBO mid is frequently a half-cent (e.g. SPY 9/18 768C mid 0.005, SPY 9/21 775C mid 0.015) and is NOT a submittable price.
findings.why_it_matters: Every limit price must be snapped to the instrument's actual tick before submission, and the direction of the snap is a real cost decision. On a $0.01-wide market a 'mid' order is impossible — you are either the bid, the offer, or rejected. If the system is ever pointed at a non-penny name, the tick becomes $0.05/$0.10 and the same code will silently submit invalid prices.
findings.source: https://www.cboe.com/notices/content/?id=57916 ; https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/cboe/2020/34-89075-ex5.pdf ; live chain metadata via broker options-chain API (2026-09-18)

findings.claim: Measured SPY/QQQ spreads: ~0.8–1.1% of mid for ATM contracts at 3–28 DTE, but 8–16% of mid for ATM 0DTE at the close, and 67%+ for cheap far-OTM contracts.
findings.detail: Snapshot taken 2026-09-18 20:14:59Z (16:15 ET, immediately after the close), SPY 762.78/762.80. SPY 28DTE 763C: 11.20/11.29 = $0.09 = 0.80% of mid. SPY 28DTE 700P (delta -0.06): 1.15/1.16 = 0.87%. QQQ 28DTE 722C: 14.05/14.20 = $0.15 = 1.06%, but ask size was 2 contracts. SPY 3DTE 763C: 1.77/1.79 = $0.02 = 1.12%. SPY 3DTE 775C (delta 0.010): 0.01/0.02 = 67% of mid. SPY 0DTE 763C: 0.12/0.13 = $0.01 = 8.0% of mid (318k volume). QQQ 0DTE 722C: 0.52/0.61 = $0.09 = 15.9% of mid, 3x3 size. This is a single instant, N=9, post-close — it is an upper bound on typical intraday spreads, not a distribution. Do not treat these as calibrated parameters; treat them as proof that percent-of-mid is the only screen that generalizes across strikes.
findings.why_it_matters: Absolute spread ($0.01) looks harmless and is catastrophic on a $0.125 option. The entry gate must be spread-as-a-fraction-of-mid, not spread in dollars, and the threshold that passes a 28DTE ATM contract will let through 0DTE garbage unless DTE-specific.
findings.source: Live option quotes via broker options-quotes API, 2026-09-18 20:14:59Z

findings.claim: 0DTE contracts go no-bid before expiry while still showing huge volume — the bid, not the spread, is the binding constraint late in the day.
findings.detail: SPY 2026-09-18 768C (≈0.7% OTM) quoted 0.00 bid / 0.01 ask with 10,951 open interest and 14,252 contracts traded that day. SPY 2026-09-18 755P quoted 0.00/0.01 with 46,912 OI and 234,188 volume. A long position in either is unsellable at any price; a short position is closeable only by paying $0.01. Note also the broker marked all same-day-expiry contracts tradability = 'position_closing_only', and returned null greeks/IV for every 0DTE contract — consistent with the known Alpaca 0DTE greeks gap.
findings.why_it_matters: Any exit logic that assumes 'I can always sell at the bid' breaks. Long 0DTE exits must be attempted while a bid still exists; the code needs a hard time-based exit, not a price-based one, and must treat bid == 0 as a distinct state (not as 'price = 0').
findings.source: Live option quotes via broker options-quotes API, 2026-09-18 20:14:59Z

findings.claim: The last trade price is not a valid pricing reference in options: complex-order legs print at prices outside the leg NBBO and still update last sale.
findings.detail: Under the Options Order Protection and Locked/Crossed Market Plan, 'Complex Trade' is an explicit exception to trade-through protection (as are crossed markets, non-firm quotes, and flickering quotes). Cboe's complex book process confirms complex orders execute at a net price bounded by the derived leg market (SBBO/SNBBO) and may 'leg in' to the simple book, so individual legs can print away from that leg's own NBBO. OPRA sale-condition codes tag these legs (L = spread leg, M = straddle leg, Q = combo, P = buy-write leg) but they are not excluded from last-sale updating — the only indicators documented as not updating open/high/low/close are out-of-hours types (EXHT) and multilateral compression (MCTP). So a 'last' of $2.00 on a contract quoted 1.50/1.60 is normal and meaningless.
findings.why_it_matters: Pricing, P&L marks, stop triggers and backtest fills must all be driven by the NBBO (bid/ask/mid), never by last/close. A stop keyed to last trade will fire on someone else's spread leg.

findings.claim: Alpaca supports no IOC and no FOK on options — only DAY and GTC. This removes the standard 'ping and cancel' execution tactic.
findings.detail: Alpaca's order documentation gives the options time-in-force matrix as GTC/DAY = yes for market, limit, stop, stop-limit; IOC, FOK, OPG, CLS = no for all types. Extended hours is not supported for options. stop and stop_limit are single-leg only. For mleg you cannot cancel or replace an individual child leg — only the whole order.
findings.why_it_matters: A price-walking algorithm must be built as submit DAY limit -> wait a bounded interval -> cancel/replace the entire order at a new price. Each replace is a race: the code must handle 'cancel rejected because already filled' and must never assume a cancel succeeded. Any design that assumed IOC slices has to be rewritten.

findings.claim: Alpaca multi-leg (mleg) orders: limit_price is the NET price, positive = debit, negative = credit; all legs must be internally covered; leg ratios must be in lowest terms; no equity legs.
findings.detail: Options Level 3 enables order_class 'mleg' with all legs filling together or not at all. Documented rejection causes: any uncovered short leg (e.g. two short calls in one order), ratio_qty values whose GCD is not 1, and any equity leg in the same order. Examples in the docs use type 'limit' with an explicit limit_price. Sign convention confirmed in Alpaca's own tutorial: credits negative, debits positive.
findings.why_it_matters: Sign errors here are a live-money bug class of their own: submitting +1.20 when you meant a $1.20 credit turns a credit spread into a debit spread at a price the market will happily fill. Build a single signing helper, unit-test it, and assert sign(limit_price) matches the strategy's expected debit/credit before every submit.

findings.claim: A true multi-leg (combo) order removes legging risk and is priced against a synthetic market derived from the legs; legging in manually is strictly worse for a retail automated system.
findings.detail: Cboe's complex book computes an SBBO (best achievable from that exchange's simple books) and SNBBO (across all markets); complex orders execute on the complex book within those derived bounds, and may leg into the simple book when that is better. Complex net prices are permitted in $0.01 increments on Cboe C1/C2/EDGX/BZX for any ratio (SPX/SPXW is the $0.05 exception), and leg execution prices are permitted in $0.01 increments in all classes. Practically this means a package can fill at a net price better than the sum of the worst leg prices, because a market maker prices the package — and it means the package either fills whole or not at all.
findings.why_it_matters: Legging a spread exposes the system to an unhedged naked leg for however long the second leg takes, which on 0DTE is the single largest tail risk in the design. Use order_class mleg for every defined-risk structure. If a combo will not fill, the correct response is to walk the net price or abandon, never to leg.

findings.claim: Alpaca paper trading fills are systematically optimistic: orders match against the NBBO with no size check, no market impact and no latency slippage.
findings.detail: Alpaca's paper-trading docs state orders are simulated against real-time quotes; a buy limit fills once its price is >= the best ask, a sell limit once <= the best bid; 'you can submit and receive a fill for an order that is much larger than the actual available liquidity'; partial fills occur for a random size only 10% of the time; and the simulator explicitly does not model 'market impact of your orders' or 'price slippage due to latency'.
findings.why_it_matters: Paper P&L on this account will overstate live P&L by roughly the execution cost of the strategy, which for 0DTE is often larger than the edge. The system must record a separate 'realistic' P&L that debits a modeled slippage per leg per fill, and promotion from paper to live must be gated on the realistic series, not the broker-reported one.

findings.claim: On the Basic (free/default) data plan, Alpaca options quotes are the 'indicative' feed — Alpaca staff describe it as 'not delayed, but adjusted' — not the OPRA NBBO.
findings.detail: Alpaca's plan comparison lists Basic (the default for paper and live) as Indicative Pricing Feed, capped at 200 websocket quote subscriptions and limited on historical data ('latest 15 minutes' restriction); Algo Trader Plus provides the OPRA feed and 1000 subscriptions. On the community forum an Alpaca engineer states the indicative option quotes 'are not delayed, but adjusted'. What 'adjusted' means precisely — which venues, what derivation — is not documented anywhere I could find. That is a real gap, not something to paper over.
findings.why_it_matters: If the bot prices off indicative quotes and believes them to be the NBBO, its mid is wrong by an unknown amount and its spread screens are measuring the wrong object. Either subscribe to OPRA before trading logic depends on quote precision, or treat indicative quotes as an estimate and widen every threshold. The code should log which feed produced each quote.

findings.claim: Crossed and locked markets, non-firm quotes and flickering quotes are recognized market states with explicit exceptions in the linkage plan — a crossed NBBO means price protection is suspended.
findings.detail: The Options Order Protection and Locked/Crossed Market Plan lists exceptions to trade-through for crossed markets, ISOs, flickering quotes, non-firm quotes, complex trades, stopped orders and benchmark trades. The rationale given for the crossed-market exception is that a Protected Bid above a Protected Offer indicates dislocation or inaccurate quoting. Separately, Cboe Rule 6.5 (obvious/catastrophic error) lets the exchange nullify or adjust an execution priced away from a 'Theoretical Price' derived from the last NBB/NBO before the trade, and contains specific machinery for determining Theoretical Price in a 'wide market'.
findings.why_it_matters: Two implications. (1) A crossed or locked NBBO is a do-not-trade state: your protections are off and the quote is probably wrong. (2) A fill that looks spectacular may be busted or repriced the next morning under Rule 6.5, so the system must not compound position size or unlock risk on the basis of an anomalous fill until it has survived the review window.

findings.claim: Options series do not all open at 9:30:00; each series opens off the first print in the underlying after 9:30 on the primary listing market, following a queuing period.
findings.detail: Cboe's opening process spec: the Queuing Period begins at 7:30 a.m.; orders and quotes on the queuing book do not participate in the opening rotation and cannot execute until the opening completes; the RTH opening for an equity option is triggered by the first transaction in the underlying on the primary listing market after 9:30 a.m. ET.
findings.why_it_matters: Quotes read in the first minutes may be pre-opening, one-sided, or from a series that has not opened. Any 'first N minutes' entry logic must verify a two-sided, non-crossed quote with a recent timestamp before acting, and should simply blackout the opening window unless the strategy specifically requires it.

findings.claim: Academic evidence says effective spreads can be well below the quoted half-spread — but only for traders who time execution, which is not what a naive marketable-limit bot does.
findings.detail: Muravyev & Pearson (Review of Financial Studies 33(11), 2020) find option price changes are predictable at high frequency and that traders who time executions pay effective spreads under 40% of conventional measures; average effective spread paid by algorithmic traders is 29.6% of the quoted half-spread versus 58.4% for all traders. This is an argument for patient, mid-anchored execution — not evidence that a retail bot will achieve those numbers. The paper's population is sophisticated algorithmic flow with sub-second timing on institutional infrastructure. A retail bot polling REST quotes over the public internet should not assume it is in that group.
findings.why_it_matters: Sets the backtest bracket honestly: optimistic bound ~30–60% of the quoted half-spread per leg, realistic base case for a marketable-limit retail bot = 100% of the half-spread per leg plus tick rounding, pessimistic = the full spread on 0DTE and near the close. Run the strategy's P&L at all three; if it only survives the optimistic one, it does not exist.

findings.claim: Share-settled SPY/QQQ options create a forced-liquidation and assignment path that the execution layer must pre-empt: Alpaca auto-exercises anything ITM by $0.01 and sells out positions it cannot fund within 1 hour of expiry.
findings.detail: Alpaca's options docs: 'By default, Alpaca will automatically exercise in-the-money (ITM) contracts at expiry'; 'the Alpaca system will exercise the contract as long as it is ITM by at least $0.01 USD'; 'In the event the account does not have sufficient buying power to exercise an ITM position, Alpaca will sell-out the position within 1 hour before expiry.' Exercise requests submitted between market close and midnight are rejected. On a ~$50k account, one exercised SPY call at ~763 is ~$76,300 of stock — far beyond the account.
findings.why_it_matters: A broker sell-out at 3:00–4:00 p.m. on expiry day happens exactly when spreads are at their worst (see the 0DTE measurements above) and at a price you do not control. The bot must close or roll every expiring position on its own schedule well before that window, and must never hold an ITM long option into the last hour unless the account can fund exercise.

findings.claim: Specific numeric liquidity thresholds (minimum open interest, minimum volume, max spread %) are not established by any authoritative source — they are engineering choices and must be labeled as such.
findings.detail: I searched for a primary or academic source establishing screen thresholds and found none. Practitioner write-ups quote figures like 'OI > 1000' or 'spread < 5% of mid' with no derivation. What the data does support: percent-of-mid is the right metric (it separated the SPY 28DTE ATM contract at 0.80% from the same-day 0DTE ATM at 8%), and top-of-book size is an independent constraint that OI and volume both miss — the QQQ 28DTE ATM contract showed 14.05/14.20 with only 2 contracts offered and 19 bid, while the SPY 0DTE 755P showed 234,188 contracts traded and no bid at all.
findings.why_it_matters: Do not hardcode thresholds and then trust them. Make every gate a named, logged, configurable constant; record the quote snapshot that passed or failed each gate on every decision; and re-fit the thresholds from your own fill data after a few hundred real orders. Volume and OI are lagging and can be high on a contract that is currently untradeable.

rules_for_the_machine: Price every order from the NBBO only. Compute mid = (bid + ask) / 2 from the current quote. Never read, store or branch on last trade price, close price, or mark for any pricing, stop, or fill decision. If a code path needs a 'price' and no two-sided quote exists, it must raise, not fall back to last.

Reject the quote and do not trade if ANY of: bid <= 0; ask <= 0; bid >= ask (crossed or locked); quote timestamp older than 2 seconds during RTH (5 seconds if using the indicative feed); the quote arrived outside 09:30:00-16:00:00 ET. Log the reason code.

Snap every limit price to the contract's own tick. Read the tick from instrument metadata at order time; do not assume $0.01. Rounding direction must always be against yourself (buy rounds down to the tick unless that makes the order non-marketable by design; sell rounds up). Assert (price * 100) % (tick * 100) == 0 before submit or refuse to send.

Never submit a market order for an option, single-leg or multi-leg, under any condition including forced exits. Forced exits use an aggressive limit at or through the opposite side with an explicit cap, never type='market'.

Gate entry on spread as a percent of mid, not dollars. Hard caps: reject if (ask - bid) / mid > 0.10 for DTE >= 7, > 0.06 for DTE 1-6, > 0.15 for 0DTE. Additionally reject any contract whose mid < $0.10 for opening trades — at that price one tick is >=10% and the spread dominates any edge.

Gate entry on displayed size, separately from volume and OI: require bid_size >= 10 and ask_size >= 10, and require the side you must eventually trade out of to show at least 3x your intended contract count. A high-volume, high-OI contract with 2 contracts on the offer fails this gate.

Gate entry on open interest >= 500 and same-day volume >= 500 on every leg. Treat these as necessary but not sufficient: they never override the live spread and size gates, which are computed from the current quote.

Use order_class='mleg' for every multi-leg structure. Legging in (submitting leg orders separately) is forbidden in code — there must be no code path that opens a defined-risk spread as two independent orders. If a combo will not fill, walk the net price or abandon the trade.

For mleg limit_price, positive = net debit, negative = net credit. Route all signing through one helper function; before submit, assert that sign(limit_price) equals the sign the strategy declared for that structure, and abort on mismatch. Unit-test both directions.

Respect Alpaca's mleg constraints as pre-submit validations: no equity legs; every short leg must be covered inside the same order; reduce all leg ratio_qty by their GCD so the GCD across legs is 1. Validate locally and fail fast rather than relying on the broker rejection.

Execution ladder for entries: start at the mid rounded to the tick in your favor; if unfilled after T seconds, reprice one tick toward the opposite side; repeat up to N steps; cap the total concession at a configured fraction of the spread (default: half the spread for DTE>=1, full spread for 0DTE exits only). Defaults: T = 3 seconds, N = 4. Abandon the trade if the cap is reached without a fill; never chase past the cap.

Implement the ladder as cancel/replace of the whole order, because Alpaca options support only DAY and GTC (no IOC, no FOK) and mleg child legs cannot be cancelled or replaced individually. Every cancel must handle the 'already filled' race: re-query order state after cancel and reconcile positions before submitting the replacement. Never submit a replacement before confirming the prior order is terminal.
Use time_in_force='day' for all options orders. Never use GTC on an options order — a resting GTC limit can fill days later on a quote the strategy never evaluated.

Treat bid == 0 as an explicit state named NO_BID, not as price zero. A long position in a NO_BID contract cannot be exited: do not compute a mid, do not attempt a sell, log it and route to the expiry handler. Never mark a position at mid when bid == 0.

Blackout windows: no new entries in the first 5 minutes after 09:30 ET (series open on the first underlying print after 9:30, off a queuing book) and no new entries after 15:45 ET. Exits are permitted in both windows.

Close or roll every position expiring today no later than 15:00 ET. Never hold an ITM long option into the last hour: Alpaca auto-exercises anything ITM by $0.01 and force-sells positions it cannot fund within 1 hour of expiry, at prices you do not control. Before 15:00, check exercise cost = strike * 100 * contracts against buying power and force the exit if it exceeds it.

Backtests and the paper-to-live promotion gate must debit modeled slippage; broker-reported paper P&L is not admissible. Alpaca paper fills at the NBBO with no size check, no market impact and no latency slippage. Per leg per fill, charge: base case = max(half_spread rounded up to one tick, 1 tick); pessimistic case = full spread for 0DTE and for any fill after 15:30 ET. Report P&L under base and pessimistic; require the strategy to be profitable under pessimistic before any live capital.
For multi-leg structures, model entry cost as the sum of per-leg half-spreads, and run a sensitivity at the sum of per-leg FULL spreads. Do not assume the combo fills at the net mid.

Record, for every order, the full quote snapshot that justified it (bid, ask, sizes, timestamp, feed name) and the actual fill price. Compute realized slippage = |fill - mid_at_decision| per leg and store it. After 200 fills, recalibrate the backtest slippage constants from this table; until then the constants are assumptions, not measurements.

Log which data feed produced each quote. If the account is on the Basic/indicative feed, multiply every spread threshold tolerance by 0.5 (be stricter) and set the staleness limit to 5 seconds — Alpaca describes indicative quotes as 'adjusted', and the derivation is undocumented, so they are not the NBBO.

Do not increase position size, unlock additional risk, or treat a strategy as validated on the basis of a single anomalously good fill. A fill priced far from the pre-trade NBBO may be nullified or repriced under exchange obvious/catastrophic error rules; quarantine such fills from sizing logic until the next session confirms them.

Kill switch: if the fraction of orders that reach the ladder cap without filling exceeds 50% over the last 20 attempts, or if realized slippage over the last 20 fills exceeds 2x the modeled base case, halt new entries and require human review. Persistent non-fill or excess slippage means the liquidity assumptions are wrong, not that the bot should try harder.

topic: Honest backtesting of options strategies from 1-minute OHLCV bars and trade prints with no historical bid/ask quotes (SPY/QQQ, Alpaca, options level 3)

findings.claim: The missing data is purchasable, and that is the only route to a defensible fill model. Alpaca itself serves historical option quotes back to Feb 2024; the free tier's quotes are explicitly NOT real OPRA quotes.
findings.detail: Alpaca's Historical Option Data doc states verbatim: "Indicative Pricing Feed is a free derivative of the original OPRA feed: the quotes are not actual OPRA quotes, they're just indicative derivatives.
