The trades are also derivatives and they're delayed by 15 minutes." and "Currently we only offer historical option data since February 2024." The `opra` feed ("the consolidated BBO feed of OPRA") is available only to subscribers; Algo Trader Plus is $99/month and includes real-time/unrestricted OPRA. Third-party historical NBBO also exists (ThetaData pairs every OPRA trade with the NBBO at trade time; Databento OPRA from 2023-03-28; Cboe DataShop sells 1-minute NBBO interval snapshots).
findings.why_it_matters: Before writing a single line of spread-reconstruction code, the system should attempt the direct fix: pull/buy real quotes for the backtest window. Any reconstruction effort is a fallback that must be labelled as such. Also: if bars were pulled on the free tier, they are derivative/delayed data, not OPRA prints — the pipeline must record and assert the feed used.

findings.claim: Filling at bar close is not a small error; it is a two-sided error worth roughly one full quoted spread of unmodelled cost per round trip, plus up to another full spread of manufactured edge for any rule that buys weakness / sells strength.
findings.detail: A bar close is a TRADE print, i.e. approximately mid ± half-spread depending on which side the last aggressor hit. (a) Cost error: a liquidity-taking bot pays ask on entry and receives bid on exit, so a close-fill backtest understates cost by ~E[half-spread] per leg per side ≈ one full spread per leg per round trip. (b) Bounce/selection error (the larger and less-known one): if the entry rule conditions on price being low (mean reversion, 'dip' adds, ladder averaging), the qualifying close is disproportionately a BID print — a price a buyer cannot get; the exit rule conditioned on price being high selects ASK prints a seller cannot get. That adds ~one more full spread of fake profit per round trip. Ladder/DCA/mean-reversion logic is maximally exposed to this. In dollars for SPY/QQQ where the tick is $0.01: each full spread ≈ $1.00 per contract per leg; a 3-rung, 4-leg structure round-tripped is on the order of $8–$24 per set of contracts of pure artefact, against credits that are often $100–$300.
findings.why_it_matters: The fill engine must never read bar.close as a fill price, and the report must show results at 1x/2x/4x assumed spread. If sign flips at 2x, the strategy is not established.
findings.source: reasoning (Roll 1984 bid-ask bounce mechanics applied to conditional entry rules)

findings.claim: SPY, QQQ and IWM quote in $0.01 increments at every premium level, so the quoted spread has a hard floor of $0.01 = $1.00 per contract, and a hard grid.
findings.detail: Under the Cboe Penny Interval Program the minimum increment is $0.01 below $3.00 and $0.05 at/above $3.00, EXCEPT that QQQ, SPY and IWM remain $0.01 regardless of price. Classes removed from the program revert to $0.05 below $3.00 / $0.10 above.
findings.why_it_matters: Gives a defensible, non-negotiable floor for the fill model and a rounding grid for all modelled bid/ask. It also means any estimator that returns a spread below $0.01 for SPY/QQQ is returning garbage and must be clamped.

findings.claim: Roll's (1984) implied-spread estimator is not usable on intraday option data. It is undefined about half the time even in its home application, and every one of its assumptions is violated here.
findings.detail: Roll infers spread from negative first-order serial covariance of price changes: S = 2*sqrt(-Cov). The empirical autocovariance is frequently positive — Roll himself hit this in roughly half his cases — leaving the estimator undefined; the common patch (drop or zero those observations) biases the survivors. Assumptions violated for 0DTE-ish ETF options: (i) trade direction is assumed serially independent, but intraday option order flow is strongly autocorrelated (momentum and order-splitting); (ii) the efficient price is assumed a random walk with no information, but the option's mid moves mechanically with delta x underlying move, which dominates the covariance; (iii) on 1-minute bars you only have OHLC, not the tick sequence Roll needs.
findings.why_it_matters: Any Roll number should be treated as, at best, a lower bound; if the fraction of undefined windows exceeds ~20%, the estimator's output must be discarded rather than patched.

findings.claim: Corwin-Schultz is downward biased exactly where you need it most — thin contracts — and its zero-truncation makes the bias worse.
findings.detail: CS assumes the period high is a buy at the ask and the low a sell at the bid, and was designed for DAILY highs/lows of continuously traded stocks. Documented problems: the high-low volatility and spread measures are downward biased with the bias concentrated in assets that do not trade continuously; negative two-day estimates are common on high-volatility days, and the standard fix (set negatives to zero before averaging) biases estimated spreads DOWN during illiquid periods. Corwin's own note addresses how to deal with negative values. On a 1-minute option bar with 1–5 prints, high==low frequently, which returns a spread of zero — a catastrophic input for a fill model.
findings.why_it_matters: CS applied naively to 1-minute option bars will systematically tell you trading is cheaper than it is, and will be most wrong on the far-OTM legs where the real cost lives.

findings.claim: EDGE (Ardia, Guidotti & Kroencke, JFE 2024) is the best available OHLC-only estimator and is the one to use if any is used — but it still estimates a WINDOW-AVERAGE effective spread of executed prints, not a per-minute quoted spread.
findings.detail: EDGE ('Efficient Discrete Generalized Estimator') estimates the effective spread from open/high/low/close under general conditions including non-frequent trading, and has reference implementations (R `bidask` on CRAN, Python port, pseudocode at bidask.eguidotti.com). Published in Journal of Financial Economics 161, 103916 (2024).
findings.why_it_matters: Use EDGE over Roll/CS where an estimate is needed, but its output can only parameterise an average cost level — it cannot produce the per-timestamp bid and ask a fill engine needs, and it cannot produce depth at all.

findings.claim: A large share of SPY/QQQ option prints are legs of complex (multi-leg) orders, which are exempt from trade-through protection and can print at prices that are not standalone-executable. This contaminates every prints-only spread estimator, biasing estimates DOWN.
findings.detail: OPRA disseminates last sale with trade condition codes; the OPRA plan codes 'L' for a leg of a spread order and 'M' for a leg of a multi-leg order. Complex trades are exempt from NBBO trade-through liability, and individual legs may print inside or outside the single-leg NBBO because the net package price is what is being satisfied. Alpaca's 1-minute option bars are OHLCV aggregates with no condition codes exposed, so leg prints cannot be filtered out of them.
findings.why_it_matters: Estimators fed on bar OHLC built from mixed single-leg and complex-leg prints are not estimating the single-leg quoted spread the bot would actually cross. With the aggregated bars alone, you cannot separate them — this is a hard 'cannot be known from the available data'.

findings.claim: Real effective spreads are materially smaller than quoted spreads for traders who time executions — but that discount is earned, not free, and must not be assumed by this system.
findings.detail: Muravyev & Pearson (RFS 2020, 33(11):4973–5014) find the average effective spread paid is 58.4% of the quoted half-spread for all traders and 29.6% for algorithmic traders, because option prices are predictable at high frequency and traders buy when fair value is near the ask. Sample: US equity options, not specifically 0DTE SPY/QQQ.
findings.why_it_matters: Two-sided implication. (1) Assuming a full half-spread cross is conservative and therefore acceptable as a base case. (2) It is NOT licence to assume mid fills: the discount comes from millisecond-scale execution timing this bot has not demonstrated. Any price improvement assumption must be earned from the bot's own recorded fills-versus-NBBO, never from this paper.

findings.claim: Modelling spread purely as a function of premium is misspecified; the dominant published driver is option return volatility (price elasticity x underlying volatility). There is no published, defensible SPY/QQQ 1-minute parameter set — it must be calibrated from your own recorded quotes.
findings.detail: The empirical literature finds option return volatility (elasticity/omega times stock return volatility) alone explains >45% of proportional bid-ask spread variation and is the single most important determinant; moneyness, time to maturity and option price matter; option VOLUME is not a significant determinant (so using volume as a liquidity proxy is unsafe). Together the determinants explain ~55% of time-series variation — i.e. ~45% is unexplained even in-sample. Practitioner-level (blog/vendor, not peer-reviewed) figures for SPY 0DTE put ATM spreads at $0.01–$0.03 and note OTM strikes widening from ~$0.05 to $0.50+ into the afternoon; treat those as anecdote, not data.
findings.why_it_matters: A defensible model form is: half_spread = max(tick/2, f(premium, |delta|, DTE, time-of-day, underlying realised vol)) with coefficients fitted to recorded NBBO. Until fitted, the constants are assumptions and the run must be labelled ASSUMED-COST and stress-tested at multiples.

findings.claim: No prints in a bar does not mean no market — and carrying the last print forward is a stale-price error that grows with delta times the underlying's move.
findings.detail: Market makers quote continuously under exchange obligations whether or not anything trades, so a zero-volume minute on a listed SPY strike is normally still tradeable. Conversely, last-observation-carried-forward on an option is wrong by roughly delta x (change in underlying) plus theta over the gap; for a 0.30-delta SPY contract and a $0.50 underlying move that is $0.15 of premium — 15 ticks, far larger than the spread being argued about.
findings.why_it_matters: Zero-print bars must be repriced theoretically off the underlying's own (well-populated) 1-minute bar with an implied-vol surface, not LOCF; and every fill occurring in a zero/low-print bar must be counted and disclosed, because it is a fill whose price rests entirely on a model.

findings.claim: Synthesizing OCC symbols for a strike grid creates two distinct biases: phantom contracts that were never listed, and — much worse — silent selection on liquidity when you drop symbols that returned no data.
findings.detail: Strike intervals for SPY/QQQ/IWM are $1 or greater (approved down to $1 above $200 for QQQ/IWM in 2019), and exchanges may open ADDITIONAL series intraday 'when the market price of the underlying security moves substantially'. So the listed grid on a given day is a path-dependent object, not a formula. The OSI symbol is 21 chars: 6-char space-padded root, YYMMDD, C/P, strike x 1000 in 8 digits; adjusted contracts carry a numeral-suffixed root (e.g. SPY1) with non-standard deliverables/multipliers. Alpaca's contracts endpoint defaults to active contracts expiring before the coming weekend and supports status=inactive plus expiration_date_lte/gte, but the docs do not explicitly guarantee full historical/expired coverage.
findings.why_it_matters: If the universe rule is 'keep symbols that returned bars', the backtest has conditioned on having traded — which is unknowable at decision time and systematically favours the strategy. Listing evidence and print evidence must be two separate, separately logged tests.

findings.claim: Alpaca paper trading cannot be used to validate the fill model — its simulator is more generous than the market in exactly the dimension being tested.
findings.detail: Alpaca's docs state paper orders are filled by simulation against real-time quotes; orders fill when marketable against the NBBO; "Your order quantity is not checked against the NBBO quantities" so you can be filled far larger than available liquidity; partial fills are injected at a random size 10% of the time; dividends and margin/short costs are not simulated; paper accounts are not charged the pass-through fees a live account pays.
findings.why_it_matters: A green paper equity curve is not evidence the spread/size assumptions are right. The only admissible calibration data are (a) NBBO snapshots the bot records at order-submission and fill time, and (b) real live fills.

findings.claim: Per-contract pass-through fees are small next to the spread but are real, are charged on both sides, and are absent from paper P&L. Index options carry much larger fees.
findings.detail: Alpaca Broker Fee Schedule (document dated updated September 1, 2026), options section: SEC Transaction Fee sells only $0.0000206 x trade value; FINRA TAF sells only $0.00329/contract; FINRA CAT buys and sells $0.000003 per equivalent share (1 contract = 100, i.e. $0.0003/contract); ORF buys and sells $0.015/contract; OCC Clearing Fee buys and sells $0.025/contract. Round trip on an equity/ETF option is therefore roughly $0.084/contract plus the SEC fee. Separately: "US-listed index options trades are subject to a $0.50 per contract fee in addition to the pass-through regulatory and exchange fees", plus an exchange table (e.g. SPXW $0.50 if premium < $1, $0.59 if >= $1; VIX $0.10–$0.45).
findings.why_it_matters: ~$0.08/contract round trip is ~8% of one penny-wide spread — not decisive, but a strategy whose edge is a few cents per contract must carry it. The index-option surcharge changes SPX-based economics entirely and must not be inherited from an SPY model.

findings.claim: American, share-settled SPY/QQQ options make expiry a real cash-flow and risk event, not a mark-to-mid close-out.
findings.detail: OCC's exercise-by-exception procedure automatically exercises options that are $0.01 or more in the money absent contrary instructions from the clearing member, though members may override in either direction. That means a long contract $0.01 ITM at settlement becomes 100 shares (~$65k of SPY exposure per contract at recent prices), and a short ITM contract becomes an assignment with overnight gap risk. Short ITM calls also carry early-assignment risk around ex-dividend when remaining extrinsic value is below the dividend.
findings.why_it_matters: A backtest that flattens everything at 16:00 at a modelled mid is claiming an exit it did not model. Pin risk (strike within a few cents of spot at the close) is genuinely unknowable from bars and must be reported as an exposure count, not priced.

findings.claim: The single hardest limitation: with prints only you can estimate an average COST LEVEL, but you cannot estimate FILL PROBABILITY or DEPTH — so any strategy that rests on resting limit orders, mid-price fills, or size is unbacktestable on this data, full stop.
findings.detail: Every estimator discussed (Roll, Corwin-Schultz, EDGE, effective-spread proxies) produces a scalar spread over a window from executed prices. None produces: the quoted bid and ask at a timestamp, the size at those prices, the queue ahead of you, or whether a passive order posted at the mid would have been filled within N seconds. A strategy simulated with 'limit at mid, assume filled' is not a backtest of that strategy; it is a backtest of a strategy nobody can run.
findings.why_it_matters: This determines strategy admissibility, not just parameters: with prints-only data, only marketable/liquidity-taking simulations are defensible, and even those only with a conservative assumed spread.

findings.claim: Bar-timestamp and intrabar-path assumptions cause larger errors than the spread question, and are silent.
findings.detail: Two classic killers: (1) using the bar in which the signal occurred as the fill bar (or mislabelling bar timestamps as end-of-bar when the API labels bar start) — a one-bar lookahead on 0DTE options can be worth more than the entire modelled edge; (2) using the bar high/low to trigger stops or take-profits — high and low are single trade prints, the intrabar path is unknown, and a level touched by one print at the bid was not necessarily executable for a seller, let alone for a buyer.
findings.why_it_matters: These are checkable with code-level lints and one calibration assertion, and should be enforced before any spread modelling work is considered meaningful.

findings.claim: What a prints-only backtest IS entitled to claim — and what it is NOT.
findings.detail: ENTITLED TO CLAIM: (a) the strategy's signal logic is implementable and produces N trades over the window; (b) directional/structural exposure statistics (time in market, delta profile, worst underlying move experienced, max concurrent contracts, margin usage); (c) an UPPER BOUND on performance, given a stated and conservative cost model; (d) sign-robustness — 'the result remains positive at 2x and 4x assumed spread' or 'it does not'; (e) failure results: if it loses money at the conservative cost assumption, that is a strong and honest negative claim. NOT ENTITLED TO CLAIM: expected live return or P&L; Sharpe, profit factor, win rate or drawdown presented as estimates of live values; anything about fill probability, passive/mid execution, price improvement, or scalability in size; per-trade edge smaller than the assumed spread uncertainty; comparative ranking of two strategies whose difference is smaller than the cost-model uncertainty; and any claim at all about legs that mostly traded in zero-print or complex-leg-contaminated bars.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the contract the report must print verbatim next to the numbers; without it the numbers will be read as forecasts.

rules_for_the_machine: DATA PROVENANCE: every stored bar/trade row must carry feed ('opra'|'indicative') and fetch timestamp. Any backtest that touches a row with feed != 'opra' aborts with an error naming the rows. Indicative data is never an input to a number that appears in a report.

NO CLOSE FILLS: the fill engine must have no code path that assigns bar.close (or vwap, open, high, low) as a fill price. Enforce with a test that mutates all close values by +50% and asserts every simulated fill price changes only through the modelled-quote path.

QUOTE MODEL REQUIRED: every fill price = round_to_tick(mid_hat +/- half_spread), buys at the ask side, sells at the bid side, never the mid. half_spread comes from the configured spread model; mid_hat comes from the repricing model, not from the last print of the decision bar.

TICK GRID: for SPY/QQQ/IWM round all modelled bids/asks to $0.01 at every premium and enforce quoted_spread >= $0.01 (half_spread >= $0.005). For any other underlying use $0.05 below $3.00 / $0.10 above unless that symbol's penny-program membership on that date is recorded in a data file with a source URL.
SPREAD FLOOR IN DOLLARS: assert modelled round-trip spread cost per contract per leg >= $1.00 for SPY/QQQ. Any configuration producing less fails validation.

CALIBRATION FLAG: the spread model config must have fields {calibrated_from: dataset id, date_range, n_observations} or calibrated_from='ASSUMPTION'. When it is 'ASSUMPTION', the run sets report.assumed_cost=true and every output file's header says ASSUMED-COST, NOT CALIBRATED.

COST SENSITIVITY IS MANDATORY: every run computes results at 1x, 2x and 4x half_spread. If the sign of net P&L flips by 4x, mark result 'not robust'. If it flips by 2x, mark 'not established' and block any promotion to a live or paper deployment path.

ESTIMATOR GATING - ROLL: compute only where the first-order autocovariance is negative; report the undefined fraction; if undefined_fraction > 0.20 the estimator output is discarded (not zero-filled, not averaged). Negative estimates are never truncated to zero and then averaged.

ESTIMATOR GATING - CORWIN-SCHULTZ: require the bar/window to have >= 20 prints and high > low; report the fraction of windows failing; if > 0.30 fail, disable the estimator for that contract-day. Prefer EDGE (Ardia/Guidotti/Kroencke) over Roll and CS where an OHLC estimator is used at all.
ESTIMATORS ARE LOWER BOUNDS ONLY: half_spread_used = max(estimator_output, tick_floor, parametric_model_output). No code path may use an estimator output directly as the fill spread.

NO ESTIMATION ON CONTAMINATED PRINTS: if the data source does not expose OPRA trade condition codes (Alpaca aggregated bars do not), complex/multi-leg legs cannot be excluded — so Roll/CS/EDGE must not be run on that source at all; the spread is recorded as 'unknown' and the parametric floor model is used.

ZERO-PRINT BARS: when a bar has trade_count == 0 or the last print is > 60s stale, mid_hat must be produced by theoretical repricing from the underlying's 1-minute bar plus an IV input, never by last-observation-carried-forward. Tag every such fill synthetic_mid=true.

SYNTHETIC-FILL DISCLOSURE: the run summary must report the share of simulated fills in bars with 0 prints and with < 5 prints. If > 10% of fills are in zero-print bars, the result is labelled 'unverifiable fills' and cannot be cited as evidence for or against the strategy.

UNIVERSE FROM THE BROKER, NOT FROM A FORMULA: only contract symbols returned by the contracts endpoint (queried with expiration_date_gte/lte covering the backtest window, status including inactive) may enter the tradable universe. A synthesized OSI string may be used to QUERY but never to TRADE. Log count of synthesized symbols rejected for lack of listing evidence.

LISTING EVIDENCE != PRINT EVIDENCE: maintain two separate exclusion counters, no_listing_evidence and zero_prints. A contract may be excluded for the first reason; it must NOT be excluded for the second (absence of prints is not absence of a market). Any code that filters the universe on volume/print-count fails review.

SYMBOL VALIDATION: reject any option symbol whose root is not exactly 'SPY' or 'QQQ' (blocks adjusted roots SPY1/QQQ1 with non-standard deliverables), and validate OSI format: 6-char space-padded root, YYMMDD, C or P, strike x 1000 zero-padded to 8 digits. Reject on any mismatch.

NO INTRABAR FILLS: stops, take-profits and triggers are evaluated only at bar boundaries against modelled bid/ask. A lint must fail the build if bar.high or bar.low is referenced anywhere inside the fill/exit engine.

NO LOOKAHEAD: decisions at bar t may read only data with timestamp <= t_start; the earliest permitted fill is bar t+1. Ship a one-time assertion test that pins the API's bar timestamp convention (start vs end) against a known market event and stores the result in the repo.

FEES ON EVERY LEG, BOTH SIDES: charge OCC $0.025 (buy+sell), ORF $0.015 (buy+sell), FINRA TAF $0.00329 (sell), CAT $0.0003 (buy+sell), SEC $0.0000206 x notional (sell). Index options additionally $0.50/contract plus the exchange table. Fee constants live in one file with effective_date and source_url; the run warns if effective_date predates the backtest end by > 12 months. Gross-of-fee equity curves may not be written to any report.

EXPIRY IS A REAL EVENT: any option >= $0.01 ITM at settlement that was not explicitly closed becomes an exercise/assignment of 100 shares per contract; model the resulting share position, its margin, and the overnight gap. Never mark an expiring position to a modelled mid and delete it. Count and report 'pin exposures' (|spot - strike| <= $0.05 at 15:59) as an unquantified risk, not a priced one.

EARLY ASSIGNMENT: for short ITM calls, flag every position held through an underlying ex-dividend date where remaining extrinsic value < the dividend, and report the count. Do not claim the backtest prices this risk.

PASSIVE EXECUTION IS OUT OF SCOPE: the simulator may only model marketable/liquidity-taking orders. Any strategy config specifying resting limit orders, mid-price fills, or price improvement is rejected at validation time with the message that fill probability cannot be estimated from trade prints.

SIZE CAP: since historical depth is unknowable, cap simulated quantity at a hard configured constant per contract class (record it as an assumption in the report) and never let modelled size scale with historical volume.

BUILD THE CALIBRATION SET FORWARD, STARTING NOW: the live/paper bot must persist an NBBO snapshot (bid, ask, bid_size, ask_size, timestamp) at every order submission and at every fill, plus 1-minute NBBO for all traded contracts. Backtests covering dates before recording began are labelled 'uncalibrated'. Only recorded NBBO or real live fills may be used to fit the spread model — paper fills may not, because Alpaca's simulator fills against NBBO with no size check and random partials.

CLAIMS BLOCK: every report must emit the explicit entitled/not-entitled claims block. A report writer must refuse to emit the strings 'expected return', 'Sharpe', 'profit factor', 'win rate' or 'drawdown' as unqualified estimates while assumed_cost=true; those metrics may only appear with the 1x/2x/4x sensitivity table adjacent and the word UPPER-BOUND on the headline number.

COMPARISONS NEED A MARGIN: two strategy variants may not be ranked unless their net-P&L difference exceeds the spread-model uncertainty band (the 1x-to-2x spread range). Otherwise the tuner must report 'indistinguishable' rather than picking a winner.

topic: 0DTE options strategy performance on SPX/SPY/QQQ — what the published evidence actually supports, and the hard constraints it implies for an automated Alpaca options-L3 system

findings.claim: SPX is not tradable on Alpaca — the system is forced into SPY/QQQ/IWM, which are American-style and physically settled. This single fact invalidates most published 0DTE research as directly applicable.
findings.detail: The account is options L3, US equities and ETFs only. Essentially all the credible 0DTE literature (Cboe, Bandi/Fusari/Renò, Dim/Eraker/Vilkov, the SPXW strategy study, Verdad) is on SPX/SPXW: European-style, cash-settled, no early assignment, no physical delivery, and favorable 1256 tax treatment. SPY/QQQ options are American-style and settle into 100 shares per contract. Practitioner sources are explicit that SPX is preferred by professional 0DTE traders precisely because cash settlement eliminates assignment and pin risk. Transplanting an SPX backtest onto SPY without modeling assignment is a category error, not a calibration detail.
findings.why_it_matters: The code must never carry a short 0DTE leg to expiration on SPY/QQQ. Every published edge estimate must be haircut for physical settlement before being used to size anything.

findings.claim: Partial-ITM pin risk lets a 'defined-risk' 0DTE spread lose MORE than its stated max loss.
findings.detail: If the underlying closes between the short and long strike, the short leg is auto-exercised (OCC exercise-by-exception at $0.01 ITM) and the long leg expires worthless. The account is left holding 100 naked shares per contract overnight with no hedge. OptionAlpha's worked example: assigned 100 SPY at $558 on a $4-wide spread; SPY opens at $550 → -$800 realized, i.e. double the spread width, with the collected credit irrelevant. There is no upper bound on this — it is bounded only by the overnight gap. OCC's $0.01 threshold is administrative and clearing members may use different thresholds, so you cannot rely on a 'close enough to the strike' assumption either.
findings.why_it_matters: Max-loss-based position sizing is WRONG for SPY/QQQ spreads held near expiry. Sizing must assume unbounded gap loss unless the position is closed before the pin window.

findings.claim: Alpaca imposes hard time cutoffs on expiration day that a 0DTE bot will hit: order submission is rejected after 15:30 ET for broad-based ETFs (15:15 ET for single names), and expiring positions are auto-liquidated starting 15:45 ET (15:30 ET single names).
findings.detail: Alpaca support states orders must be submitted before 3:15 p.m. ET for stocks/options and before 3:30 p.m. ET for broad-based ETFs like SPY and QQQ, and that orders placed after these times will be rejected. Expiring positions are auto-liquidated starting 3:30 p.m. ET (options) / 3:45 p.m. ET (broad-based ETFs). Automatic exercise of ITM-by-$0.01 positions occurs by 6:00 p.m. ET. If the account lacks buying power to exercise an ITM long, Alpaca sells it out within 1 hour before expiry — at whatever price it gets.
findings.why_it_matters: The last ~45 minutes of the session — where most 0DTE gamma P&L happens — is unavailable to this system. Any strategy whose expectancy depends on holding into the close is not implementable here, and broker-initiated liquidation at an uncontrolled price is a real, modelable cost.

findings.claim: Alpaca L3 does not permit any uncovered short option, and a multi-leg order is rejected unless every leg is covered within that same order. Rolling and equity legs are not supported.
findings.detail: Alpaca: "We support all level 3 strategies. However, at this time, we do not support any uncovered short options strategies." Docs: "An MLeg order is accepted only if all its legs are covered within the same MLeg order" — an MLeg with two short call legs is rejected; this also blocks rolling a short contract and calendar spreads. MLeg orders containing an equity leg are not supported. All ratio_qty values must reduce to GCD 1. Examples use limit orders, day TIF.
findings.why_it_matters: The order-construction and exit logic must be written around this: you cannot leg in, cannot roll in one order, and an exit that closes the long wing first will be rejected or leave a naked short.

findings.claim: The best available academic estimate is that the 0DTE variance risk premium is real but economically small, and unconditional 0DTE short-premium strategies lose money on average after realistic execution.
findings.detail: A systematic study of SPXW 0DTE payoffs across seven structures (straddles, strangles, iron butterflies, iron condors, risk reversals, vertical spreads, ratio spreads), 09/2016–01/2026 (~9.3 years), concludes: "All the strategies reap negative returns on average," distributions are "wide, state-dependent, and dominated by tail risk rather than by stable mean carry," and unconditional 0DTE "is difficult to justify as a standing allocation once one accounts for realistic execution and downside capital usage." The positive VRP contributes only about 0.20% of spot even in extreme scenarios. OptionMetrics independently measures SPX 0DTE VRP (10:00 ET ATM implied variance minus forecast realized) at mean 0.0028 / median 0.0021 in variance units — small. Dim/Eraker/Vilkov reach the same conclusion: positive but small and "difficult to monetize after realistic frictions."
findings.why_it_matters: The system must be built on the assumption that gross edge is roughly zero and that costs decide the outcome. Any component that assumes 'theta is free income' is a bug.

findings.claim: Iron butterflies — the most-marketed 0DTE structure — went NEGATIVE after costs in the same study that produced the headline Sharpe numbers.
findings.detail: In the conditional out-of-sample implementation: put ratio spreads gross SR 1.18 → 0.93 net; strangles gross 0.56 → 0.39 net; iron butterflies gross SR 0.77 but "turn negative after costs." An equal-weight basket of ALL strategies: gross 0.81 → net 0.25. Top-three-by-net-Sharpe basket: gross 1.12 → net 0.82. Note these are the CONDITIONAL results (with a directional classifier); unconditionally the same structures are negative. Execution assumption was half-spread plus 0.5bp — optimistic for a retail API account.
findings.why_it_matters: Cost modeling is not a refinement, it is the difference between a positive and negative Sharpe. Any backtest marked at mid is meaningless and must be rejected as a basis for going live.

findings.claim: The win-rate/payoff-ratio arithmetic of 0DTE short premium is brutal and is where most strategies die. Observed win rates sit BELOW the break-even win rate implied by the payoff ratio.
findings.detail: Concrete published example (SPX 0DTE iron butterfly, 254 trades, Jan 2024–Oct 2025): 2024 win rate 77%, avg win ~$200, avg loss ~$800 → break-even win rate = 800/(800+200) = 80%. Result: +$5,079. 2025 win rate 78%, avg win ~$200, avg loss ~$1,500 → break-even = 1500/1700 = 88.2%. Result: -$5,472. Two-year net: roughly flat, after a headline '431% annualized' first year. Separately, Option Alpha's 230,000 REAL 0DTE executions (Sep 2021–Aug 2023, 81% SPY / 13% QQQ) show iron condors 70.19% win, iron butterflies 66.76% win — and only 49.64% of the trader population was profitable overall. A 10-delta 2-wide SPY condor collecting $0.25 needs ~87.5% wins just to break even before costs.
findings.why_it_matters: The code must compute break-even win rate = max_loss/(max_loss+credit) at entry and compare it to the strategy's own rolling realized win rate. If realized < break-even, the strategy is losing money regardless of how good the win rate 'feels'.

findings.claim: 'Theta decay is not free' is not a slogan — it is an identity. The P&L of a delta-hedged short option over an interval is 0.5·Γ·S²·(realized variance − implied variance)·dt. Theta is the payment for gamma, nothing more.
findings.detail: Under the risk-neutral measure the expected P&L of any option position is zero. The entire edge of a short 0DTE position is the gap between the implied variance you sold at and the variance that actually realizes over the holding period, scaled by gamma and dollar-squared spot. Because 0DTE gamma is enormous and grows through the day, the variance term dominates: the study above finds ex-post strategy P&L "loads more on directional and skewness realizations than on realized variance alone," meaning even the VRP framing overstates how clean the harvest is. There is also a measurement trap: 0DTE implied vol is dominated by jump-risk premium, and realized vol computed at standard sampling frequencies does not capture the same time scale — so naive IV-minus-RV comparisons overstate the premium.
findings.why_it_matters: Pre-trade logic must estimate today's expected intraday realized vol and require entry IV to exceed it by a margin. Without that check the system is selling variance at random prices and calling the credit 'income'.
findings.source: reasoning (Black-Scholes delta-hedged P&L identity), corroborated by https://github.com/vilkovgr/0dte-strategies/blob/main/docs/paper/paper-annotated.md and https://optionmetrics.com/blog/the-0-dte-variance-premium-mag7-reward-more-and-punish-harder/

findings.claim: Transaction costs on a four-leg SPY 0DTE structure plausibly consume 15–35% of gross credit — far larger than commissions, which are near zero.
findings.detail: Alpaca charges no options commission but passes through: ORF $0.015/contract (buys and sells), OCC clearing $0.025/contract (buys and sells, up to 2,750 contracts), FINRA TAF $0.00329/contract (sells only), CAT ~$0.000003/equivalent share. For a 1-lot iron condor that is roughly $0.33 round trip in fees total — negligible. The real cost is spread: SPY 0DTE bid/ask is typically $0.01–$0.03 wide, so 4 legs × ~$0.01 half-spread × 2 (in and out) ≈ $0.08/share = $8 per condor. Practitioner backtest convention is to assume $0.05 slippage on entry AND exit. Against a typical $0.20–$0.30 credit ($20–$30) on a $2-wide condor, $8 of round-trip spread is 27–40% of gross credit. Note: 'slippage is negligible' claims in practitioner content are made about 1-lot SPX with penny-wide quotes and do not generalize to a 4-leg SPY structure executed by an API at scale.
findings.why_it_matters: A cost gate must run pre-trade off live NBBO and veto entries where modeled round-trip cost exceeds a fixed fraction of the net credit. This is the single highest-leverage check in the system.

findings.claim: Time-of-day effects are real in VOLATILITY but the evidence for a profitable entry-time rule is weak and largely practitioner marketing.
findings.detail: What is well supported: intraday realized vol on heavy 0DTE sessions is elevated at the open and the close (U-shape), and Cboe confirms dealer net gamma range "grows wider as the day progresses." What is NOT well supported: that any specific entry clock time carries positive expectancy. The SPXW study's appendix finds patterns "qualitatively unchanged" across 16:00 prior-day, 13:00 and 15:00 ET entries — i.e., entry time was not the driver. Option Alpha's real-execution data shows profitable trades averaged ~10:15 ET entry and ~12:00 ET exit (~2h hold) and that Monday/Wednesday were positive while Thursday/Friday were negative — but this is in-sample descriptive statistics on self-selected user trades with no multiple-testing correction, and the authors note trades were "indiscriminately chosen, with complete disregard to things like overlapping strikes and portfolio risk." Treat day-of-week results as noise until replicated.
findings.why_it_matters: Entry-time windows should be used as RISK controls (avoid the open's spread blowout and the close's gamma), not as alpha. Do not let the optimizer fit a clock time.

findings.claim: Tail risk is measured and it is large: 1% expected shortfall runs 0.58–1.58% of the UNDERLYING notional per position, and single worst-day losses dwarf average carry.
findings.detail: The SPXW study reports 1% expected shortfall of "roughly 0.58–1.58% of underlying" across the seven strategy families, and states "maximum single-day losses are severe; worst-case outcomes dwarf average carry." It also finds equal-weighting across strategies "does not eliminate tail risk" — it only smooths strategy-specific drawdowns. Verdad's construction, which is the most bullish credible case for selling 0DTE, still sizes to only 16 basis points of portfolio so that a 10% intraday S&P move costs 2% of the portfolio, and notes such a move has not occurred in 30 years — i.e. the strategy is only defensible at tiny size.
findings.why_it_matters: Sizing must be driven by tail loss on underlying notional, not by the spread's nominal max loss, and the total notional the bot controls must be capped explicitly.

findings.claim: The bullish case for selling 0DTE (Verdad) is coherent but rests on a model assumption, not on measured returns.
findings.detail: Verdad concludes 0DTE options are "overpriced by roughly 0.75–1.0 vol points" from a market-maker equilibrium model, and derives an expected 1.6% annual portfolio return with Sharpe 0.85–1.4 from a 16bp allocation to short 0DTE straddles, assuming 15% implied vs 14.25% fair vol under Black-Scholes. This is a modeled expectancy, not a realized track record, and it is directly contradicted on realized data by the SPXW study ('all strategies reap negative returns on average') and by Dim/Eraker/Vilkov ('small and difficult to monetize after realistic frictions'). Note also that a 1.6% annual portfolio return from a 16bp allocation is a huge return ON the allocated capital but a trivial contribution to a portfolio — the honest reading is 'a small, fragile carry trade', not 'an income strategy'.
findings.why_it_matters: Do not use Verdad's Sharpe numbers as a sizing input. They are a theoretical upper bound under a model, at a position size 100x smaller than what a $50k 0DTE bot would typically run.

findings.claim: The documented blow-up mode is not a gap overnight — it is intraday, and it is 'letting the trade work out'.
findings.detail: Because 0DTE gamma is extreme, a defined-risk short structure can traverse from small profit to full max loss in minutes without any gap. Practitioner consensus, and the pattern in the loss data above, is that an iron butterfly at -2x credit by midday on expiration day essentially never recovers. Concrete stress dates: 5 Aug 2024 (vol spike; credit spreads repriced to >$6 net premium), 4 Apr 2025 (-4.5% day) and the April 2025 tariff sequence (S&P -5.97% on the China retaliation day). Early Retirement Now, running a long-horizon SPX 0DTE/1DTE short-put book, reports ~$13k of early-April 2025 losses before recovering, and describes the April 2025 intraday volatility as something he hopes will not repeat. His stated lesson is specific and implementable: replace stop-LOSS with stop-LIMIT orders, because "during a flash-crash, when liquidity dries up, you might get fills at outrageous prices," and "never sell positions you couldn't hold to expiration" if stops fail.
findings.why_it_matters: Stop logic must be stop-limit with a defined buffer, must fire mechanically, and sizing must survive the stop failing entirely.

findings.claim: The one genuinely credible long-horizon practitioner track record is more modest than it looks and is not reproducible on Alpaca.
findings.detail: Early Retirement Now 2025: $103,700 of options income on ~10,000 contracts and $6.5bn notional, premium capture rate 74.2% overall — but 0DTE puts captured only 62.2% and 0DTE calls only 53.1%, while the 1DTE puts (94% PCR, $55k+) carried the book. Losses occurred on 8 put days and 6 call days. Sizing guidance: $170k–$200k of portfolio value per short overnight put. Two problems for this system: (a) most of the profit came from the OVERNIGHT 1DTE leg, not from 0DTE, and (b) the sizing implies a ~$50k account can carry well under one contract by his own rule. It is also SPX, cash-settled, with no 15:30 broker cutoff.
findings.why_it_matters: The most-cited real 0DTE success story is mostly a 1DTE overnight short-put story at institutional sizing. Do not let the bot infer that 0DTE intraday selling on $50k reproduces it.

findings.claim: The other side of the trade — buying 0DTE — is documented as a reliable loser, which is the strongest single piece of evidence that a premium exists at all.
findings.detail: Beckmeyer, Branger & Gayda find >75% of retail S&P 500 option trades are 0DTE, retail is predominantly net LONG, and retail lost approximately $184k per day across Feb 2021–Feb 2023 (Verdad cites $358k/day, ~$90M/year, since May 2022 from the same work). Bogousslavsky & Muravyev find 0DTE trades underperform other option trades by 3%. Cboe reports 0DTE grew from 5% of SPX volume in 2016 to 63–65% of SPX volume by Feb–May 2026, with 0DTE ADV of 3.1M contracts in Q2 2026. Important caveat: 'buyers lose' does NOT mean 'sellers net win' — the losses accrue substantially to market makers' spread capture and fees, not to a directional seller taking unhedged risk.
findings.why_it_matters: Justifies a short-premium prior, but only weakly. The bot is not a market maker and does not capture the spread — it PAYS it. That is the gap between 'retail buyers lose $90M/yr' and 'my condor is profitable'.

findings.claim: The 'dealer gamma / 0DTE destabilizes the market' narrative is not supported by the data, and a strategy built on gamma-flow signals is building on sand.
findings.detail: Cboe's own study: on a day with 100k+ contracts on a single strike, market makers were left short only ~3k contracts (52k bought vs 55k sold) — 3% of gross volume. Dealer net gamma ranged $170mm–$670mm intraday, median +$173mm at 15:30, equal to 0.04%–0.17% of daily S&P futures liquidity. Close-to-close vs intraday realized vol spread was 2.7 vol points YTD, exactly the 10-year average. Dim, Eraker & Vilkov independently find high 0DTE open-interest gamma "does not propagate past volatility" and intraday 0DTE volume shocks do not amplify recent index returns. Commercial GEX/gamma-flow products are marketing, not evidence.
findings.why_it_matters: Do not wire third-party dealer-gamma or GEX signals into entry logic. There is no published evidence they predict anything.

findings.claim: Single-name 0DTE variance premium is much larger but has strongly NEGATIVE skew — the opposite risk profile from the index.
findings.detail: OptionMetrics, 399 Friday expirations: TSLA VRP mean 0.0315, NVDA 0.0161, AMZN 0.0111, AAPL 0.0089 vs SPX 0.0028 (TSLA ~11x the index). But skewness is negative for single names (-0.45 to -4.14) versus POSITIVE (+1.33) for SPX. Their conclusion: "single-name short volatility appears lucrative on average, but the asymmetric downside risk warrants caution for any strategy seeking to harvest it systematically." Negative VRP skew means occasional episodes where realized variance massively exceeds implied — exactly the scenario that kills a short-premium book.
findings.why_it_matters: A fat single-name premium will look attractive to any optimizer. It must be hard-blocked, not left to a risk score.

findings.claim: Where the evidence is genuinely thin or absent, and the honest answer is 'unknown'.
findings.detail: (1) There is NO peer-reviewed study of 0DTE short-premium performance on SPY or QQQ specifically, net of physical-settlement assignment costs. Every quantitative result cited here is SPX. (2) There is no credible published evidence that any entry-time, day-of-week, or technical filter produces out-of-sample positive expectancy on 0DTE after costs; the one study that reports conditional Sharpes uses a directional classifier whose out-of-sample validity cannot be verified from the public artifact. (3) There is no published measurement of what a $50k retail API account actually achieves in fill quality on 4-leg 0DTE MLeg orders — all cost estimates here are modeled. (4) Optimal stop-loss and profit-target levels for 0DTE are entirely un-established in the literature; the widely cited '2x credit stop' and '15%/-25%' figures come from vendor blogs fitting in-sample. (5) Whether the 0DTE premium survives the growth from 5% to 65% of SPX volume is untested — the sample is short and dominated by a low-realized-vol regime.
findings.why_it_matters: The system must be built to MEASURE these things on paper before any of them is trusted, and must refuse to treat a fitted parameter as a known quantity.
findings.source: reasoning over the full source set

rules_for_the_machine: INSTRUMENT WHITELIST: 0DTE short-premium entries are permitted only on SPY, QQQ, IWM. Hard-reject any 0DTE multi-leg short-premium order on a single-name underlying (including all MAG7), on grounds of negative VRP skew (OptionMetrics: single-name VRP skew -0.45 to -4.14 vs SPX +1.33). Implement as an allowlist, not a scoring penalty.

NO EXPIRATION CARRY, EVER: every 0DTE position must be fully flat by 15:00 ET. Emit a WARN at 14:45 ET if any 0DTE position is open, force an unconditional market-crossing close attempt at 15:00 ET, and treat failure to be flat by 15:20 ET as a P1 alert plus a trading halt for the rest of the day. Never allow the strategy to rely on Alpaca's 15:45 ET auto-liquidation or on expiry settlement.

RESPECT ALPACA CUTOFFS AS HARD CONSTANTS: no order submission after 15:30 ET for SPY/QQQ/IWM (15:15 ET for single names) — orders are rejected by the broker. Store these as named constants with the source URL in a comment, and assert at startup that the configured flatten time is at least 30 minutes before them.

PIN-RISK GUARD: from 14:00 ET onward, on every cycle, if spot is within max(1.0 x current ATR(5min), 0.5 x wing width) of ANY short strike in an open position, close that position immediately at market-crossing limits regardless of P&L. Log the event. Rationale: partial-ITM assignment converts a defined-risk spread into a naked overnight 100-share position whose loss is unbounded (documented example: -$800 on a $4-wide spread).

NEVER CREATE AN UNCOVERED SHORT: all opens and closes must be submitted as a single MLeg order containing every leg. If a partial fill or a broker rejection ever leaves a short leg without its cover, immediately close the short leg first (never the long leg first) and raise a P1 alert. Assert before every order that no permutation of partial execution leaves a naked short. Alpaca rejects uncovered short strategies outright, so a naked leg means the position cannot be managed normally.

PRE-TRADE COST GATE (highest-priority check): compute modeled round-trip cost = sum over legs of (ask-bid)/2, times 2 for entry+exit, plus per-contract fees (ORF $0.015 both sides, OCC $0.025 both sides, TAF $0.00329 sells, CAT negligible). Reject the entry if modeled_round_trip_cost / net_credit > 0.15. Log the computed ratio on every entry, accepted or rejected. Quote must be a live NBBO snapshot less than 2 seconds old.

NO MARKET ORDERS ON MULTI-LEG 0DTE, EVER, INCLUDING EXITS. Use limit MLeg orders. Entry: start at mid, reprice toward the natural at most 3 times at 5-second intervals, then cancel. Exit: start at mid, step toward the natural every 3 seconds, but cross the full spread if not filled within 30 seconds — an unfilled 0DTE exit is a larger risk than the spread cost.

STOP-LIMIT, NOT STOP-LOSS: every protective exit must be a stop-limit with the limit placed a defined buffer (minimum 3 ticks) beyond the stop, never a bare stop. Documented practitioner failure mode: in a liquidity vacuum a market stop fills at outrageous prices. Additionally, log every stop trigger and compute a rolling false-stop rate (stops that would have recovered); if false-stop rate exceeds 50% over 40 trades, raise the stop distance or halt the strategy for review.

SIZE ON TAIL LOSS, NOT ON SPREAD MAX LOSS: per-position underlying notional must satisfy 0.0158 x notional <= 0.5% of account equity, using the published 1% expected-shortfall upper bound of 1.58% of underlying. On a $50k account this caps notional at roughly $15,800 per position (about 25 SPY shares-equivalent, i.e. well under one 1-lot at SPY ~$600 — meaning the honest output of this rule is that $50k supports at most one small defined-risk spread at a time). Do not override this with the nominal max loss of the spread.

PORTFOLIO CAPS: total simultaneous defined max loss across all open 0DTE positions <= 2% of account equity; single-position defined max loss <= 0.5% of equity. Additionally cap the number of concurrent 0DTE positions at 2, and forbid two positions with overlapping short strikes on the same underlying (the Option Alpha dataset explicitly warns its results ignored overlapping strikes and portfolio risk).

BREAK-EVEN WIN-RATE MONITOR: at entry compute required_win_rate = max_loss / (max_loss + net_credit). Persist it. Maintain a rolling realized win rate over the trailing 60 closed trades. If realized_win_rate < required_win_rate (averaged over those trades) for 10 consecutive trading days, halt the strategy and require human re-approval. This is the check that would have caught the published iron-fly case (78% realized vs 88% required in 2025).

VARIANCE-EDGE PRECONDITION: do not open a short-premium 0DTE position unless entry ATM implied vol exceeds a forecast of today's intraday realized vol by a configured minimum margin (start at 1.0 vol point). Use a documented forecast (e.g. prior-day intraday squared-log-return realized vol, the OptionMetrics methodology) and log implied, forecast, and the realized outcome for every trade so the premise can be tested. If the margin cannot be computed, do not trade. Rationale: delta-hedged short-option P&L = 0.5 x Gamma x S^2 x (realized_var - implied_var) x dt; there is no other source of edge.

INTRADAY LOSS CIRCUIT BREAKERS: halt all new entries and close all open 0DTE positions if any of the following fire — (a) cumulative day P&L <= -1.5% of account equity; (b) two consecutive trades hit full stop; (c) SPY moves more than 1.5% from the prior close intraday; (d) SPY 5-minute return exceeds 4 standard deviations of its trailing 20-day 5-minute distribution. Weekly halt at -4% of equity requiring human re-approval to resume.

EVENT BLACKOUT: no 0DTE entries on FOMC decision days before 14:30 ET, and none within 30 minutes either side of scheduled CPI, PPI, NFP, or PCE releases. Maintain the calendar as data, fail closed (no trade) if the calendar is stale by more than 24 hours.

ENTRY WINDOW IS A RISK CONTROL, NOT ALPHA: permit entries only between 10:00 and 13:30 ET. Do not let any optimizer tune the entry clock time, day-of-week filter, or expiry weekday — the published evidence that these carry expectancy is in-sample and uncorrected for multiple testing. Hard-code the window and record it as a risk decision.

BAN DEALER-GAMMA / GEX SIGNALS from entry logic. Cboe's own data shows median dealer net 0DTE gamma of +$173mm at 15:30 (0.04-0.17% of S&P futures liquidity) and market makers left holding 3% of gross volume; Dim/Eraker/Vilkov find 0DTE gamma does not propagate volatility. Any commercial gamma-flow feed may be logged for research but must not gate an order.

BACKTESTS MUST BE MARKED TO EXECUTABLE PRICES: any backtest used to justify a parameter change must fill sells at the bid and buys at the ask (not mid), include the full fee schedule, and simulate the 15:00 ET forced flatten. A mid-marked backtest must be rejected by the research pipeline with an explicit error. The published evidence is that iron butterflies flip from gross Sharpe 0.77 to negative purely on cost treatment.

ASSIGNMENT DETECTION AND RECOVERY: after every fill and at 16:15 ET and 09:25 ET daily, reconcile Alpaca positions against the internal ledger. If an unexpected equity position appears (assignment), raise a P1 alert immediately, block all new option entries, and flatten the shares at the next regular-session open with a limit order. Never let the bot silently carry assigned shares.

DO NOT EXTRAPOLATE SPX RESEARCH TO SPY/QQQ WITHOUT A HAIRCUT: every parameter imported from a published SPX study must be tagged in config with its source and a flag indicating it is unvalidated on physically-settled ETFs. Require a minimum 100-trade paper track record on the actual SPY/QQQ implementation, with realized win rate, realized payoff ratio, realized cost-to-credit ratio, and realized IV-minus-RV all logged, before any parameter is promoted to a live-capital configuration. There is no published study of 0DTE short premium on SPY/QQQ net of assignment.

NO SIZE ESCALATION AFTER LOSSES: position size must be a pure function of account equity and the tail-loss rule above. Explicitly forbid martingale, averaging down into a losing 0DTE structure, rolling out a tested side, or adding a second position to 'repair' the first. Note also that Alpaca's MLeg coverage requirement makes rolling a short contract impossible in a single order, so any repair logic would transiently create a naked short.

VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME, REGULATORY STATE AT STARTUP: query the account's actual day-trade / PDT status, options level, and buying power from the Alpaca API on every start rather than assuming the PDT repeal or level 3 approval applies. Fail closed and refuse to trade if options_approved_level < 3, if the account is flagged in any restricted state, or if the API call fails.

HUMAN GATE ON REAL MONEY: this system stays on the paper account. Any transition to live capital requires an explicit, separate human action outside the codebase — no configuration flag, environment variable, or agent decision may switch the account endpoint. Assert at startup that the base URL is the paper endpoint and abort otherwise.

topic: Computing option greeks and implied volatility locally when the broker supplies none, with correct handling of 0DTE

findings.claim: Alpaca structurally cannot return greeks or IV for 0DTE contracts, and also drops them whenever its own solver fails — so the gap is wider than 'same-day expiry'.
findings.detail: Alpaca's Market Data FAQ states greeks require ALL of: non-zero bid AND ask on the latest contract quote; a latest SIP trade for the underlying; "the contract expiration is after today"; and "the calculated implied volatility is valid". Alpaca computes greeks with Black-Scholes via the Go `gopriceoptions` package with "a maximum of 100 iterations. If the calculated price does not converge...then no implied volatility is calculated." So greeks vanish not only on expiry day but on any contract with a zero bid (very common for far-OTM 0DTE and for wings on any expiry), and on any contract whose IV solve does not converge in 100 iterations. This is a data-plan-independent limitation: "The issue is not the data plan, but rather how Alpaca calculates these values."
findings.why_it_matters: The code must treat broker greeks as an optional, frequently-absent field, never a required one. It must have a local engine that is the primary source, with broker greeks used only as a cross-check — and it must never silently substitute a stale or missing greek with zero.

findings.claim: Option price, spot delta and gamma depend on T and sigma ONLY through total variance w = sigma^2 * T. Therefore the choice of clock (calendar vs trading time) is irrelevant for delta/gamma when IV is solved from the same quote with the same clock — but it is decisive for theta and for any cross-expiry IV comparison.
findings.detail: Write w = sigma*sqrt(T). Then d1 = [ln(F/K) + w^2/2]/w, d2 = d1 - w, and the Black-76 price is exp(-rT)*[F*N(d1) - K*N(d2)]. If you rescale the clock T -> a*T, the sigma you solve from the same market mid becomes sigma/sqrt(a), w is unchanged, d1/d2 are unchanged, and the price, spot delta (exp(-qT)N(d1)) and gamma are unchanged to within the negligible exp(-rT)/exp(-qT) factors at short T. What DOES change: vega scales by sqrt(a), theta (per wall-clock unit) scales by 1/a, and the printed IV number scales by 1/sqrt(a) — so a 0DTE IV computed on a business-minute clock (Cboe VIX1D convention) is about sqrt(525600/102060) = 2.27x the same option's IV computed on a calendar-minute clock (Cboe VIX convention). This is an algebraic identity, not an empirical claim.
findings.why_it_matters: Stop agonizing over the clock for hedging/sizing (delta and gamma are safe either way). DO enforce one global clock constant, refuse to compare IVs computed under different clocks, and never publish a theta number without stating the clock. A term-structure or 'is 0DTE IV rich' signal built from mixed clocks is off by up to 2.3x.
findings.source: reasoning (algebraic identity), with the two clock constants verified against Cboe methodology documents

findings.claim: Cboe itself uses two different clocks: calendar minutes (525,600/yr) for VIX, and BUSINESS minutes (252 x 6.75 x 60 = 102,060/yr) for the 1-day index VIX1D. For a same-day-expiry product, the exchange's own choice is trading time, not calendar time.
findings.detail: Cboe Volatility Index Mathematics Methodology, sec. 3(a)(i): "The Cboe volatility index calculation measures time to expiration of a constituent option series, T, in calendar years... by dividing the number of minutes until expiration of the selected options (rounded down to the nearest minute) by the number of minutes in a year... (365 x 1,440 = 525,600)." The 2009 VIX white paper gives T = {M_currentday + M_settlementday + M_otherdays}/525,600, with M_settlementday = minutes from midnight to 8:30 a.m. Chicago for AM-settled SPX and 900 minutes (3:00 p.m. Chicago = 4:00 p.m. ET) for PM-settled. By contrast the Cboe 1-Day Volatility Index methodology states: "The calculation of the VIX1D Index uses business years and business minutes during the Regular Trading Hours (RTH) session... the time component for the VIX1D Index is measured in a different increment than the VIX Index, which uses calendar years and calendar minutes", with "Number of business minutes during RTH session in a year (252 x 6.75 x 60 = 102,060)".
findings.why_it_matters: Pick business minutes (102,060/yr) for anything 0DTE/short-dated so that the IV number is comparable to how 0DTE vol is actually quoted and so overnight gaps are not mispriced as 'a full day of decay'. Hard-code both constants and tag every stored IV with which one was used.

findings.claim: Cboe stops recomputing the near-term 0DTE variance once fewer than 60 business minutes remain, and freezes the last valid value. An exchange with unlimited engineering resources concluded the 1/T term is untrustworthy in the last hour.
findings.detail: VIX1D methodology: "when the time to expiration for the near-term (current day expiry) is less than 60 business minutes (at approximately 3:00 p.m. ET), the single-term volatility of the near term will be the last valid value and persisted until the near-term expiration time", and the index then interpolates with weights "heavily concentrated on the next-term". After the near-term expires at ~4:00 p.m. ET the near leg is dropped entirely and "the formerly persisted near-term volatility will not be used".
findings.why_it_matters: Implement an explicit last-hour regime: after T_business < 60 minutes, freeze or heavily damp the IV input, and switch position risk from greek-based to terminal-payoff-based. Do not let a freshly-solved 3:55pm IV drive sizing.

findings.claim: Solve for total variance w = sigma*sqrt(T), not for sigma. This removes the T->0 ill-conditioning entirely, because d(price)/dw = S*exp(-qT)*phi(d1) does NOT collapse to zero as T->0 for near-the-money strikes, whereas vega = S*exp(-qT)*phi(d1)*sqrt(T) does.
findings.detail: Newton on sigma uses the step sigma_{n+1} = sigma_n - (BS(sigma_n) - P_mid)/vega(sigma_n). As T->0 vega -> 0 like sqrt(T), so the step blows up and the iteration diverges or oscillates. Reparameterising to w: w_{n+1} = w_n - (BS(w_n) - P_mid)/(S*exp(-qT)*phi(d1)), then sigma = w/sqrt(T) at the end. The w-vega is bounded and well-behaved at ATM regardless of T. This is the same normalization that makes Jaeckel's 'Let's Be Rational' converge to machine precision in about two iterations for all inputs; that paper exists specifically because "near intrinsic value, near expiry, and in deep wings, small price perturbations can correspond to large volatility changes".
findings.why_it_matters: A direct, testable implementation change: the solver's state variable should be w (or ln w), with sigma derived at the end. It is the single highest-value numerical fix for 0DTE.
findings.source: http://www.jaeckel.org/LetsBeRational.pdf (algorithm), reasoning for the w-reparameterisation identity

findings.claim: Even with a perfect solver, the $0.01 price tick puts a hard floor on IV resolution at 0DTE. Near the close, one tick of price is worth several volatility points, so the solved IV is quantization noise.
findings.detail: IV resolution per tick = tick / vega_per_unit_vol, where vega_per_unit_vol (per share) = S*exp(-qT)*phi(d1)*sqrt(T). Worked example, SPY at S=600, ATM (phi(d1)=0.3989), business-minute clock (102,060 min/yr): with 60 minutes left, T=5.88e-4, sqrt(T)=0.02425, vega=5.80 per unit vol -> 1 cent of price = 0.0017 vol = 0.17 vol points. With 5 minutes left, T=4.90e-5, sqrt(T)=0.00700, vega=1.68 -> 1 cent = 0.60 vol points. With 1 minute left, vega=0.75 -> 1 cent = 1.3 vol points. On a CALENDAR clock the same option at 1 minute has vega=0.33 -> 1 cent = 3.0 vol points. And the binding constraint is usually not the tick but the quoted spread: a 3-cent-wide 0DTE ATM quote at 5 minutes to expiry means the IV is only pinned to about +/- 1 vol point, and at 1 minute to about +/- 2 to 4 vol points.
findings.why_it_matters: The code must carry an IV uncertainty band, computed as (half_spread / vega), and must refuse to act on any IV-derived signal whose band exceeds a threshold. 'IV solved successfully' is not the same as 'IV is meaningful'.
findings.source: reasoning (closed-form vega with realistic SPY inputs)

findings.claim: Gamma at 0DTE is genuinely enormous and is NOT a numerical artifact — but it means a stale underlying price corrupts delta far faster than a wrong IV does.
findings.detail: gamma = exp(-qT)*phi(d1)/(S*sigma*sqrt(T)) per share. SPY S=600, sigma=0.20 (business clock), 5 minutes left: sigma*sqrt(T)=0.20*0.00700=0.0014, gamma = 0.3989/(600*0.0014) = 0.475 per $1 per share, i.e. a $1 move changes delta by 47 points; per contract that is 47.5 deltas. At 1 minute, gamma ~ 1.06/share. Consequence: if the underlying quote used in the greek calc is 2 seconds stale and SPY has moved $0.03, the delta error is 0.03*0.475 = 0.014 (1.4 delta points) at 5 minutes and ~3 points at 1 minute; on a fast tape with a $0.20 move the delta error is 10 to 20 points. Alpaca's own greeks use "latest (SIP) trade for the underlying symbol" — a trade print, which can be off-mid and stale.
findings.why_it_matters: Enforce a timestamp-coherence check between the option quote and the underlying quote before computing any greek, and prefer the underlying NBBO mid over the last trade so the option mid and the underlying are measured the same way.

findings.claim: Do not model dividends or the risk-free rate for the underlying at all. Extract the option-implied forward from put-call parity at the ATM strike and price with Black-76. This is exactly what Cboe does, and it absorbs dividends, borrow cost, and rate error into one observable.
findings.detail: Cboe Mathematics Methodology: "Determine the option-implied forward price level, F, by identifying the options strike price at which the absolute difference between the call price and the put price is smallest... F = Strike Price + e^(RT) * (Call Price - Put Price)", where call/put prices are bid/ask midpoints; series with null quotes or crossed quotes (bid > ask) are disqualified from being the ATM strike. Then price with Black-76: d1 = [ln(F/K) + w^2/2]/w, d2 = d1 - w, w = sigma*sqrt(T); C = exp(-rT)*[F*N(d1) - K*N(d2)], P = exp(-rT)*[K*N(-d2) - F*N(-d1)]. Spot delta = exp(-qT)*N(d1) for a call; if you work in F, forward delta = N(d1) and spot delta = (F/S)*exp(-rT)*N(d1) to first order. For a discrete-dividend ETF the continuous-yield q is simply wrong over a short horizon; the forward is right by construction.
findings.why_it_matters: Eliminates an entire class of bugs (wrong q, wrong r, wrong ex-date calendar) and makes the model self-consistent with the quotes you actually trade against. Requires a parity-quality gate: both ATM legs must have two-sided, uncrossed quotes.

findings.claim: The right risk-free rate source is the U.S. Treasury daily par yield curve (CMT), with a documented BEY -> APY -> continuously-compounded conversion. But at 0DTE the rate is almost irrelevant, while at 30-45 DTE it is not.
findings.detail: Cboe: "The risk-free interest rate, R, is calculated based on U.S. Treasury yield curve rates... constant maturity Treasury (CMT) yields (i.e., bond equivalent yields) available on the U.S. Treasury website. Next a cubic spline is applied to interpolate/extrapolate a yield for each date between maturities, the bond equivalent yields (BEY) are converted to annualized percentage yields (APY), and then these yields are converted to continuously compounded interest rates." The conversion is explicit: APY = (1 + BEY/2)^2 - 1, then R = ln(1 + APY). (The 2009 white paper used the T-bill BEY closest to expiry; the current methodology uses the CMT spline.) Treasury publishes these daily from quotations "obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York at approximately 3:30 PM each business day". Magnitude check: rho = K*T*exp(-rT)*N(d2). SPY-like K=600, ATM: at T = 1 day, rho ~ 600*0.004*0.5 = 1.2 per unit r, so a 100bp rate error moves the price by 1.2 cents per share. At T = 45 days (T=0.123), rho ~ 36.9, so a 100bp error moves the price by 37 cents per share (~$37/contract).
findings.why_it_matters: For the 0DTE path, a stale or even zero rate is tolerable and must not be a blocker. For any 30-45 DTE credit-spread path, the rate must be fresh (same business day) or the forward must be taken from parity instead. Code the two paths differently and say so.

findings.claim: American early exercise makes BSM wrong in two specific, boundable ways — and for 0DTE both bounds are small enough to ignore, which is the opposite of the usual intuition.
findings.detail: Merton (1973): an American call on a non-dividend-paying underlying is never optimally exercised early, so BSM is exact for it. Two rigorous error bounds apply generally: (a) American call - European call <= PV(dividends with ex-date strictly before expiry); (b) American put - European put <= K*(1 - exp(-rT)). At 0DTE with r=4%, business T = 1/252 year: K*(1-exp(-rT)) = 600*0.000159 = $0.095/share — i.e. the entire early-exercise premium on a 0DTE put is bounded by under 10 cents per share, and is near zero for anything not deep ITM. With no ex-date before expiry, bound (a) is exactly zero. At 45 DTE the put bound rises to 600*(1-exp(-0.04*0.123)) = $0.29/share, still modest. So the European approximation is fine for pricing and greeks; the American feature matters for ASSIGNMENT RISK, not for the model.
findings.why_it_matters: Stop trying to build a binomial/American solver for 0DTE — it buys nothing. Spend that effort on the assignment-risk calendar instead. Do add an assertion that the two bounds above are recomputed and logged so the approximation error is always known rather than assumed.
findings.source: reasoning from Merton (1973) early-exercise results, with numeric bounds computed here

findings.claim: SPY goes ex-dividend on quarterly option-expiration Fridays, which is precisely when ITM short calls get assigned early. The 2026 SPY ex-dates are 3/20, 6/18, 9/18 and 12/18 — and 9/18/2026 is today.
findings.detail: State Street's official 2026 SPDR Dividend Distribution Schedule lists SPY (quarterly) with Ex Date = Record Date on 3/20/2026, 6/18/2026, 9/18/2026, 12/18/2026, plus a 12/31/2026 potential excise distribution. All four are third Fridays. Cboe's own education material: SPY options "are American style, meaning the option owner may choose to exercise ahead of expiry. This often occurs in advance of the quarterly ex-dividend date" and "if an option is in the money going into the ex-dividend date and the dividend exceeds the remaining time value of the option, the call owner likely has economic incentive to exercise their options early." Decision rule for the bot: a short ITM call is at material early-assignment risk when Dividend > remaining_time_value, where remaining_time_value = call_mid - max(0, S - K), evaluated on the LAST trading session before the ex-date.
findings.why_it_matters: A hard calendar gate: on the session before an ex-dividend date, screen every short call leg for time_value < dividend and either close it or pre-provision for assignment. This is a directly implementable check and it is the main way an ETF dividend actually costs money — not through the pricing model.

findings.claim: Solve IV only from OUT-of-the-money options and map to the ITM twin by put-call parity. ITM American quotes carry early-exercise premium and can sit outside the European price range, where no BSM root exists at any sigma.
findings.detail: European no-arbitrage range for a put is max(0, K*exp(-rT) - S*exp(-qT)) < P < K*exp(-rT). An American put may legitimately trade at or near intrinsic K - S. Whenever K - S >= K*exp(-rT) — i.e. deep ITM with meaningful r*T — the quoted mid sits at or above the European upper bound and the solver has NO root: Newton will run to the sigma ceiling and either return the ceiling (garbage) or fail. Even short of that, the root is biased high. OTM options have no early-exercise premium to speak of and their prices are strictly monotone in w across the whole usable range. Parity then gives the ITM side: C - P = exp(-rT)*(F - K).
findings.why_it_matters: Implement as a routing rule in the solver, not a patch: choose put if K < F, call if K >= F, solve, then derive the twin. This alone removes most real-world 'IV solve failed' events.
findings.source: reasoning from standard no-arbitrage bounds and Merton (1973)

findings.claim: Newton-Raphson alone is not acceptable; a bracketed safeguarded solver is. Price is strictly increasing in w, so a bracket always exists when the target is inside the no-arbitrage range, and bisection can never fail.
findings.detail: Recommended structure: (1) validate the target mid against the no-arbitrage bounds; (2) bracket w in [w_lo, w_hi] with w_lo ~ 1e-8 and w_hi grown by doubling from an initial guess until BS(w_hi) > target or w_hi implies sigma > 5.0 (500%); (3) run safeguarded Newton (Newton step accepted only if it lands inside the current bracket, otherwise bisect) on w with analytic derivative S*exp(-qT)*phi(d1); (4) stop when |BS(w) - target| < 0.25 * tick OR bracket width < 1e-10, with an absolute cap of 50 iterations. Pure bisection converges in ~50 iterations from a wide bracket; safeguarded Newton typically converges in 3-6. A 500% sigma ceiling is not excessive for far-OTM 0DTE strikes in the last hour — those legitimately imply several hundred percent annualised vol on a calendar clock.
findings.why_it_matters: Every branch is testable: bounds-check, bracket-found, converged, iteration-cap-hit. Each failure mode gets its own reason code rather than a silent NaN.
findings.source: reasoning; failure characteristics corroborated by http://www.jaeckel.org/LetsBeRational.pdf

findings.claim: When IV cannot be solved, there is a genuinely model-free substitute for the one greek that matters most: risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM, read off adjacent strikes.
findings.detail: dC/dK = -exp(-rT)*N(d2), so N(d2) ~ exp(rT) * (C(K - dK) - C(K + dK)) / (2*dK) using the same-expiry neighbouring strike mids. At 0DTE and near ATM, N(d1) and N(d2) are both close to 0.5 and differ by roughly phi(0.5)*w, which is tiny when w is tiny — so this estimator is also a serviceable delta proxy exactly in the regime where the IV solve is worst. It requires no volatility input at all and no sigma. Its failure mode is the opposite of the solver's: it degrades when neighbouring strikes are illiquid or the strike grid is coarse, not when T is small.
findings.why_it_matters: Gives the code a defined fallback rather than a hole: if IV solve fails but two neighbouring strikes have two-sided quotes, use the finite-difference N(d2) for gating and sizing, and flag the value as 'model-free proxy' so downstream logic knows vega/theta are unavailable.
findings.source: reasoning (Breeden-Litzenberger first derivative); the second-derivative density version is standard, the first-derivative delta proxy is being recommended here as an engineering fallback rather than cited from a source

findings.claim: Alpaca's own expiration-day behaviour imposes operational deadlines that matter more than any greek: opening orders stop at 3:30 p.m. ET, ITM-by-$0.01 longs are auto-exercised, and positions are liquidated if buying power is short.
findings.detail: Alpaca docs: "Starting at 3:30 pm EST on the date of expiration, Alpaca continuously evaluates any open positions that expire that day and stops accepting new orders to open/extend any positions." Alpaca auto-exercises longs ITM by $0.01 or more given sufficient buying power (calls) or shares (puts); "If there is not enough buying power or shares, then Alpaca will liquidate while it's still ITM." For covered calls and cash-secured puts ITM by $0.01+, "Alpaca will automatically assign after close on date of expiry." DNE instructions are accepted "until 4:30 pm ET". The $0.01 threshold is the OCC exercise-by-exception level for equity and index options, though clearing/brokerage firms may use different values.
findings.why_it_matters: The bot needs wall-clock gates independent of the pricing model: no new 0DTE opens after 15:25 ET (buffer before Alpaca's 15:30 cutoff), and a pre-close sweep that computes intrinsic against a $0.01 threshold and forces a close or DNE rather than relying on a delta estimate.

findings.claim: EVIDENCE IS WEAK on the exact expiry instant for SPY/QQQ options on their own expiration day. Secondary sources say 4:15 p.m. ET normally and 4:00 p.m. ET on the last trading day; Cboe's own hours page confirms a 4:15 p.m. core session but says nothing about expiration day.
findings.detail: Cboe's US options hours page gives "Core Trading Session 9:30 a.m. 4:15 p.m." for BZX/C2/EDGX options and does not address the last-trading-day case for SPY/QQQ/IWM. Multiple secondary sources assert that on the last trading day these close at 4:00 p.m. ET. Cboe's VIX1D methodology independently confirms that the PM-settled SPX (SPXW) 0DTE contracts expire "typically at 4:00 p.m. ET", and the 2009 VIX white paper uses 3:00 p.m. Chicago (= 4:00 p.m. ET) as the PM settlement instant — but SPXW is a different product from SPY. I did not find an exchange rule filing confirming the SPY/QQQ expiration-day close.
findings.why_it_matters: Do not hard-code 16:15. Make the expiry instant a per-symbol configuration value defaulting to 16:00:00 ET, clamp T at zero below it, and log the assumption. A 15-minute error in the expiry instant at 15:55 is a 100% error in remaining time and therefore a ~41% error in the solved IV and in vega.
findings.source: https://www.cboe.com/about/hours/us-options (core session only); expiration-day close asserted only by secondary sources

findings.claim: The standard normal CDF must be computed via erfc, not a polynomial approximation, because 0DTE lives in the far tail where cheap approximations lose all their accuracy.
findings.detail: Use N(x) = 0.5*erfc(-x/sqrt(2)). At 0DTE, |d1| and |d2| routinely exceed 5 for strikes only a dollar or two away from spot, and can exceed 20. Abramowitz-Stegun style rational approximations are accurate to ~1e-7 absolute, which is meaningless when the true value is 1e-12 — the relative error is total, and it propagates directly into the OTM price and hence into the solver's residual. Also: phi(x) = exp(-x^2/2)/sqrt(2*pi) underflows to exactly 0 for |x| beyond about 38-39 in double precision. Guard gamma and vega so that a zero phi produces an exact zero rather than a 0/0 NaN when combined with a near-zero sigma*sqrt(T) denominator.
findings.why_it_matters: Two concrete code requirements: use math.erfc, and add explicit underflow guards on every expression with phi(d1) in the numerator and sqrt(T) or sigma*sqrt(T) in the denominator.
findings.source: reasoning (IEEE754 double-precision limits and standard error bounds of A&S 26.2.17)

findings.claim: Mid price is the wrong IV target whenever the quote is one-sided, crossed, or wider than the information it contains — Cboe's own index methodology simply refuses to compute rather than using such a quote.
findings.detail: Cboe Mathematics Methodology disqualifies series where "quotes... are null or the bid price is higher than the ask price", excludes any option with a zero bid or zero ask, and states that if the qualifying set is exhausted "the Cboe volatility index cannot be calculated" — an explicit refusal path rather than a degraded number. It also runs a series-level outlier detection and quote-filtering algorithm before using any quote. Practical translation for a single contract: reject the quote if bid <= 0, or ask <= 0, or bid > ask, or ask/bid ratio exceeds a threshold on cheap options, or the quote timestamp is older than a staleness limit, or half_spread/vega exceeds the IV tolerance.
findings.why_it_matters: Gives a directly copyable validation ladder with a defined terminal state ('cannot be calculated') that the strategy layer must handle, instead of a fabricated number.

rules_for_the_machine: Never require broker-supplied greeks. Alpaca returns none when expiration is today, when either side of the contract quote is zero, when there is no latest SIP underlying trade, or when its 100-iteration IV solve fails. The local engine is the source of truth; broker greeks may only be logged as a cross-check and must never be substituted in when the local value is missing.

Define exactly two clock constants and use one globally per computation path: MINUTES_PER_CALENDAR_YEAR = 525600 and MINUTES_PER_BUSINESS_YEAR = 102060 (252 * 6.75 * 60). Use the business clock for all 0DTE and short-dated work.
